ENG-01.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask for the kind of a noun, the plural of irregular words (datum, crisis, mother-in-law), the feminine of a masculine noun, and nouns that are always singular or always plural.

## Kinds of noun
A **noun** is the name of a person, place, thing, quality or idea.

| Kind | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Proper** | Name of a particular person/place/thing (capital letter) | Dhaka, Rabindranath, the Padma |
| **Common** | Name shared by every member of a class | boy, city, river, book |
| **Collective** | Name of a group taken as one whole | army, team, jury, family, class, committee, herd, flock |
| **Material** | Name of a substance (usually uncountable) | gold, water, rice, milk, iron |
| **Abstract** 🔥 | Name of a quality, state or action (cannot be touched) | honesty, childhood, freedom, beauty, laughter |

- **Countable** nouns have a plural (pen/pens); **uncountable** nouns don't (water, advice).
- Proper → common: "He is **the Newton** of our college" (= a great scientist). "Dhaka is **the London** of Bangladesh."
- Material/abstract as common: "a **stone**", "**kindnesses**", "**youths**" (= young men).

### Abstract nouns from other words 🔥
| Word | Abstract noun | Word | Abstract noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| child | **childhood** | brave | **bravery** |
| friend | **friendship** | wise | **wisdom** |
| slave | **slavery** | high | **height** |
| thief | **theft** | poor | **poverty** |
| king | **kingdom / kingship** | long | **length** |
| hero | **heroism** | free | **freedom** |
| live | **life** | choose | **choice** |
| know | **knowledge** | believe | **belief** |

## Number
### Regular rules
- add **-s/-es**: book → books; box → boxes; hero → **heroes**, potato → **potatoes**; but photo → **photos**, piano → **pianos**, radio → radios.
- consonant + y → **-ies** (lady → ladies); vowel + y → -s (day → days).
- -f/-fe → **-ves** (knife → knives, leaf → leaves, wolf → wolves); but **roof → roofs, chief → chiefs, proof → proofs, belief → beliefs, safe → safes**.

### Irregular and foreign plurals 🔥
| Singular | Plural | Singular | Plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| man | **men** | **datum** | **data** |
| foot | **feet** | **medium** | **media / mediums** |
| tooth | **teeth** | **memorandum** | **memoranda** |
| mouse | **mice** | **phenomenon** | **phenomena** |
| ox | **oxen** | **criterion** | **criteria** |
| child | **children** | **crisis** | **crises** |
| **formula** | **formulae / formulas** | **analysis** | **analyses** |
| **radius** | **radii** | **basis** | **bases** |
| **alumnus** | **alumni** | **thesis** | **theses** |
| **stimulus** | **stimuli** | **hypothesis** | **hypotheses** |
| **index** | **indices / indexes** | **axis** | **axes** |
| **bureau** | **bureaux / bureaus** | **cherub** | **cherubim / cherubs** |
| **agendum** | **agenda** | **oasis** | **oases** |

### Compound nouns 🔥
The **main word** takes the plural: **mothers-in-law, sons-in-law, commanders-in-chief, passers-by, men-of-war, courts-martial**. Exceptions: **spoonfuls, handfuls**. man/woman as first word: **men-servants, women-doctors**.

### Same form in singular and plural
**sheep, deer, swine, fish** (usually), **aircraft, series, species, salmon**. Numbers after a figure: **two dozen eggs, five hundred taka, a ten-mile walk, a five-year plan** (no -s).

### Always plural (take plural verb)
**scissors, trousers, spectacles, tongs, pliers, thanks, alms, riches, premises, cattle, people, police, poultry, gentry, clergy**. "The **police have** arrested him." "**Cattle are** grazing."

### Look plural but singular 🔥
**news, physics, mathematics, economics, politics** (as a subject), **measles, mumps, billiards**. "**The news is** good." "**Mathematics is** my favourite."

### Always singular (uncountable, no -s) 🔥
**information, advice, furniture, luggage, baggage, scenery, machinery, poetry, equipment, bread, knowledge, mischief**. Say "a piece of advice", "an item of furniture" — **never "advices", "furnitures", "sceneries"**.

## Gender
| Masculine | Feminine | Masculine | Feminine |
|---|---|---|---|
| bachelor | **spinster / maid** | fox | **vixen** |
| drake | **duck** | gander | **goose** |
| stag | **hind** | horse | **mare** |
| bull/ox | **cow** | colt | **filly** |
| dog | **bitch** | cock | **hen** |
| hero | **heroine** | lad | **lass** |
| tiger | **tigress** | lion | **lioness** |
| wizard | **witch** | monk | **nun** |
| nephew | **niece** | sir | **madam** |
| emperor | **empress** | sultan | **sultana** |
| **testator** | **testatrix** | executor | **executrix** |
| **drone** | **bee** | peacock | **peahen** |
| **earl** | **countess** | beau | **belle** |

- **Common gender:** both sexes — parent, child, friend, teacher, student, baby, cousin, person.
- **Neuter:** lifeless things — book, table.
- Personification: **sun, death, time, war** → masculine (he); **moon, earth, nature, ship, country, peace** → feminine (she).

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He gave me many advices. | He gave me **much advice / many pieces of advice**. |
| The furnitures are new. | The **furniture is** new. |
| The news are true. | The news **is** true. |
| I bought two dozens eggs. | I bought **two dozen** eggs. |
| My mother-in-laws are kind. | My **mothers-in-law** are kind. |
| The cattle is grazing. | The cattle **are** grazing. |
| The scenery of Sylhet are charming. | The scenery **is** charming. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Plural of **datum = data**, **criterion = criteria**, **phenomenon = phenomena**, **crisis = crises**.
- 🔥 **mother-in-law → mothers-in-law**; **passer-by → passers-by**.
- **advice, information, furniture, scenery, luggage** are uncountable: no -s.
- **news, physics, mathematics** take singular verbs.
- **cattle, police, people** take plural verbs.
- Feminine of **fox = vixen**, **drake = duck**, **stag = hind**, **bachelor = spinster**.
- Abstract noun of **child = childhood**, **thief = theft**, **wise = wisdom**.

ENG-02.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask which period a writer belongs to, the name and dates of an age, and who the age is named after ("Age of Chaucer", "Age of Pope", "Age of Johnson").

## The periods at a glance 🔥
Dates are the ones used in most exam guides; historians round them slightly differently.

| Period | Approx. dates | Key writers / works |
|---|---|---|
| **Old English (Anglo-Saxon) Period** | **450–1066** | ***Beowulf***, Caedmon, Cynewulf, Bede, King Alfred |
| **Middle English Period** | **1066–1500** | **Chaucer**, Langland (*Piers Plowman*), Gower, *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight*, Malory |
| — **Age of Chaucer** | **1340–1400** | *The Canterbury Tales* |
| **Renaissance Period** | **1500–1660** | Includes the Elizabethan, Jacobean and Caroline ages |
| — **Elizabethan Age** | **1558–1603** | **Shakespeare, Spenser, Marlowe**, Sidney, Bacon |
| — **Jacobean Age** | **1603–1625** | **Ben Jonson, Donne**, Webster; **King James Bible (1611)** |
| — **Caroline Age** | **1625–1649** | Cavalier poets (Herrick, Lovelace, Suckling), metaphysical poets |
| — **Commonwealth / Puritan Age** | **1649–1660** | **Milton** (prose), Marvell, Hobbes |
| **Restoration Period** | **1660–1700** | **Dryden** (Age of Dryden), Bunyan, Congreve, Milton's *Paradise Lost* (1667) |
| **Neo-classical / Augustan Age** | **1700–1745** | **Pope, Swift, Addison, Steele, Defoe** (Age of Pope) |
| **Age of Johnson / Age of Sensibility** | **1745–1798** | **Dr. Johnson, Goldsmith, Richardson, Fielding**, Gray, Burke |
| **Romantic Period** | **1798–1832** | **Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats**, Scott, Jane Austen, Lamb |
| **Victorian Period** | **1832–1901** | **Tennyson, Browning, Arnold, Dickens, the Brontës, George Eliot, Hardy** |
| **Modern Period** | **1901–1939** (to c. 1945) | **Yeats, T. S. Eliot, Joyce, Woolf, Lawrence, Conrad, Shaw** |
| **Post-modern / Contemporary** | **1945–present** | Beckett, Osborne, Larkin, Ted Hughes, Golding |

## Key turning points 🔥
- **1066**: Norman Conquest → end of Old English, start of Middle English (French influence).
- **1476**: **William Caxton** set up the **first printing press in England** (Westminster). He printed *The Canterbury Tales* and Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485).
- **1558**: Queen Elizabeth I comes to the throne.
- **1642**: theatres closed by the Puritans; reopened in **1660** at the Restoration of Charles II.
- **1798**: ***Lyrical Ballads*** by **Wordsworth and Coleridge** → start of the Romantic Movement.
- **1832**: First **Reform Act**, and death of Sir Walter Scott → end of the Romantic age.
- **1837**: Queen Victoria crowned; **1901**: she dies.

## Ages named after writers 🔥
| Name of age | Writer |
|---|---|
| **Age of Chaucer** | Geoffrey Chaucer (14th century) |
| **Age of Shakespeare** | Elizabethan age |
| **Age of Milton** | Puritan age |
| **Age of Dryden** | Restoration (1660–1700) |
| **Age of Pope** | Augustan / Neo-classical (1700–1745) |
| **Age of Johnson** | 1745–1798 |
| **Age of Wordsworth** | Romantic age |
| **Age of Tennyson** | Victorian age |

## Other names you must know
- **Augustan Age**: the early 18th century, named after Roman emperor Augustus, whose age produced Virgil, Horace and Ovid. Writers copied classical models, so it is also called **Neo-classical**.
- **Age of Reason / Age of Prose and Reason**: 18th century (reason over emotion).
- **Golden Age of English literature / drama**: **Elizabethan Age**.
- **Age of Transition**: the later 18th century (Gray, Collins, Cowper, Blake, Burns), which prepared the way for Romanticism. Poets of this group are called **pre-Romantics**.
- **Renaissance** = "rebirth" (of classical learning). It began in **Italy** (14th century) and reached England in the 16th century.

## Main features by period
| Period | Features |
|---|---|
| Old English | Alliterative verse, heroic epic, Christian and pagan elements |
| Middle English | Romance, allegory, French influence, Chaucer's realism |
| Elizabethan | Drama at its peak, sonnet, blank verse, patriotism |
| Restoration | Comedy of manners, satire, heroic couplet, reason |
| Augustan | Satire, periodical essay (*The Tatler*, *The Spectator*), rise of the novel |
| Romantic | Nature, imagination, emotion, the common man, the supernatural |
| Victorian | Social problems, science vs faith, realism, the novel dominant |
| Modern | Stream of consciousness, free verse, alienation, experiment |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Old English: **450–1066**; Middle English: **1066–1500**.
- 🔥 Elizabethan Age: **1558–1603**; Romantic Age: **1798–1832**; Victorian Age: **1832–1901**.
- Romanticism started with ***Lyrical Ballads* (1798)**.
- **Caxton** brought printing to England in **1476**.
- **Age of Pope** = Augustan / Neo-classical age.
- Restoration = **1660**, when Charles II returned; the age of **Dryden**.
- **Beowulf** is the chief Old English work.

ENG-03.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams test the right case (I/me, who/whom), the pronoun after "than/as/between/let", the order "you, he and I", and agreement with "each, everyone, neither".

## Kinds of pronoun
| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Personal** | I, we, you, he, she, it, they (and me, us, him, her, them) |
| **Possessive** | mine, ours, yours, his, hers, theirs |
| **Reflexive / Emphatic** | myself, yourself, himself, itself, ourselves, themselves |
| **Demonstrative** | this, that, these, those, such |
| **Interrogative** | who, whom, whose, which, what |
| **Relative** | who, whom, whose, which, that |
| **Indefinite** | one, none, any, some, somebody, everyone, all, few |
| **Distributive** | **each, either, neither** |
| **Reciprocal** | **each other** (two), **one another** (more than two) |

- **Reflexive:** the action comes back to the subject: "He hurt **himself**."
- **Emphatic:** only for emphasis: "I **myself** saw it."
- "**Hisself**", "**theirselves**", "**ourself**" (in ordinary use) are wrong.

## Case rules 🔥
- **Subject** of a verb → nominative (I, he, she, we, they, who).
- **Object** of a verb or **preposition** → objective (me, him, her, us, them, whom).
  - "**Between you and me**" (not "between you and I").
  - "**Let him and me** go." ("let" takes object pronouns.)
  - "It is **I**." / "It was **he**." (formal: after the verb *be*, nominative).
- **After than / as**, supply the missing verb in your head:
  - "He is taller **than I** (am)."
  - "I love you more **than him**" (= than I love him) ≠ "more **than he**" (= than he loves you).
  - "She is as clever **as he** (is)."
- **Who vs whom:** "**Who** do you think is right?" (subject of *is*). "**Whom** did you meet?" (object of *meet*).

## Order of personal pronouns 🔥
- Good things: **2nd, 3rd, 1st** → "**You, he and I** are friends." (231)
- Admitting fault / blame: **1st, 2nd, 3rd** → "**I, you and he** are to blame." (123)

## Agreement with the antecedent 🔥
A pronoun agrees with its **antecedent** (the noun it replaces) in number, gender and person.

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| **each, every, either, neither, everyone, anyone, no one, somebody** → singular | "**Each** of the boys has done **his** duty." "**Everyone** must do **his** (or his or her) duty." |
| **one** → one's | "**One** should do **one's** duty." (not *his* in strict usage) |
| Two singulars joined by **and** → plural | "**Rahim and Karim** have done **their** work." |
| Two singulars by **or / nor / either…or / neither…or** → singular | "**Either Rahim or Karim** has lost **his** pen." |
| Same person described by two nouns with one article | "**The secretary and treasurer** has resigned **his** post." (one person) |
| Collective noun as one unit → it | "**The jury** gave **its** verdict." |
| Collective noun as members → they | "**The jury** were divided in **their** opinions." |
| **each other** (two) / **one another** (many) | "The two brothers love **each other**." "The students helped **one another**." |

## Relative pronoun points
- **who** for persons, **which** for things/animals, **that** for both.
- Use **that** (not *who/which*) after a **superlative**, **all, same, only, any, nothing, none**: "He is **the best** man **that** I know." "**All that** glitters is not gold."
- Use **whose** for possession: "the boy **whose** father is a doctor".
- Verb after a relative pronoun agrees with its antecedent: "It is **I who am** to blame." "He is **one of the boys who are** clever." (antecedent = boys).

## "None", "such", "same"
- **none** → usually plural in modern use with countables, but exams often prefer **singular** with "none of … is"; both are accepted.
- Avoid using "**such**" or "**same**" as a pronoun in letters: "Please send **them**" (not "send the same").

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| Between you and I. | Between you and **me**. |
| Let you and I go. | Let you and **me** go. |
| He is taller than me. (formal writing) | He is taller than **I** (am). |
| I, you and he are friends. | **You, he and I** are friends. |
| Each of the girls have done their work. | Each of the girls **has** done **her** work. |
| Whom do you think is coming? | **Who** do you think is coming? |
| He hurt hisself. | He hurt **himself**. |
| The two sisters love one another. | The two sisters love **each other**. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 "Between you and **me**"; "Let **him and me** go".
- 🔥 Order: good = **you, he and I**; fault = **I, you and he**.
- **each/every/either/neither** → singular verb and pronoun.
- **each other** = two; **one another** = more than two.
- Use **that** after superlatives and "all".
- "It is **I who am** …" — verb agrees with the antecedent.
- **One** takes **one's**.

ENG-04.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about *Beowulf* (hero, monster, language, period), Chaucer's epithets and *The Canterbury Tales* (number of pilgrims, tales, the Wife of Bath), and other early works.

## Old English period (450–1066)
- Language: **Old English (Anglo-Saxon)**, brought by the Angles, Saxons and Jutes.
- Verse is **alliterative** (repeated initial sounds), with a **caesura** (pause) in the middle of each line; no rhyme.
- Four main manuscripts survive; *Beowulf* is in the **Cotton Vitellius A.xv** (Nowell Codex).

### Beowulf 🔥
| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Genre | **Oldest surviving epic in English** / the national epic of the Anglo-Saxons |
| Length | About **3,182 lines** |
| Author | **Unknown (anonymous)** |
| Date | Composed c. **8th century** (some say 7th–10th); manuscript c. 1000 |
| Setting | **Denmark and Sweden (Geatland)** — not England |
| Hero | **Beowulf**, a prince of the **Geats** |
| Danish king helped | **Hrothgar**, whose mead-hall is **Heorot** |
| Monsters | **Grendel**, **Grendel's mother**, and a **dragon** |
| Ending | Beowulf, now old king of the Geats, kills the dragon but **dies**; his young follower **Wiglaf** helps him |

### Other Old English writers
| Writer | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Caedmon** | **First known English poet**; "Caedmon's Hymn"; called the "Father of English song" |
| **Cynewulf** | Signed his poems in runes; *Elene*, *Juliana*, *Christ II* |
| **The Venerable Bede** | ***Ecclesiastical History of the English People*** (written in **Latin**, 731); "Father of English history" |
| **King Alfred the Great** | **Father of English prose**; translated Latin works; began the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* |
| Elegies | *The Wanderer*, *The Seafarer*, *The Wife's Lament* |

## Middle English period (1066–1500)
- After the **Norman Conquest (1066)**, French became the language of the court; English absorbed many French words.
- Key works:
  - ***Sir Gawain and the Green Knight*** — Arthurian romance by the anonymous **Pearl Poet (Gawain Poet)**.
  - ***Piers Plowman*** — allegory by **William Langland**.
  - ***Confessio Amantis*** — **John Gower** ("moral Gower", Chaucer's friend).
  - ***Le Morte d'Arthur*** — **Sir Thomas Malory**, printed by **Caxton in 1485**.
  - **John Wycliffe** — first complete translation of the **Bible into English** (1380s); "Morning star of the Reformation".
  - **Mystery, Miracle and Morality plays**, e.g. ***Everyman***.

## Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) 🔥
### Epithets
- **"Father of English poetry"** — **Dryden** called him this.
- **"Father of English literature"** (common exam answer; some guides also give **"Father of the English language"**).
- **"Well of English undefiled"** — **Spenser** called him this.
- Do not confuse: **"Morning star of the Reformation"** is **John Wycliffe**.
- He was the **first poet buried in Poets' Corner**, Westminster Abbey.

### Works
| Work | Fact |
|---|---|
| ***The Canterbury Tales*** 🔥 | His masterpiece; unfinished; written in the **heroic couplet** (mostly) in the **East Midland (London) dialect** |
| ***Troilus and Criseyde*** | Long love poem in **rhyme royal**; set in Troy |
| ***The Book of the Duchess*** | Elegy for Blanche, wife of John of Gaunt |
| ***The House of Fame***, ***The Parliament of Fowls*** | Dream-vision poems |
| ***The Legend of Good Women*** | Stories of faithful women |
| *Treatise on the Astrolabe* | Prose, scientific |

### The Canterbury Tales 🔥
- **Pilgrims** go from the **Tabard Inn** in **Southwark (London)** to the shrine of **Saint Thomas Becket** at **Canterbury**.
- The **General Prologue** introduces **29 pilgrims** (plus Chaucer himself; the Host **Harry Bailey** is the 31st). Most guides say **"29 pilgrims"**.
- Plan: each pilgrim tells 2 tales going and 2 returning (about 120 tales). Chaucer finished only **24 tales**.
- Famous characters: **the Knight** (first tale), **the Wife of Bath** (married five times), **the Prioress (Madame Eglantine)**, **the Pardoner**, **the Miller**, **the Clerk of Oxford**, **the Summoner**, **the Monk**, **the Friar**, **the Nun's Priest** (Chanticleer the cock).
- Opening line: **"Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote…"**
- Chaucer's Knight is described as **"a verray, parfit gentil knyght"**.

### Chaucer's three periods
| Period | Works |
|---|---|
| **French** | *The Book of the Duchess* |
| **Italian** | *Troilus and Criseyde*, *The House of Fame*, *The Parliament of Fowls* |
| **English** (mature) | ***The Canterbury Tales*** |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 *Beowulf*: oldest English epic, anonymous, hero a **Geat**, monsters **Grendel**, his mother and a **dragon**.
- 🔥 Chaucer: **"Father of English poetry"**.
- *The Canterbury Tales*: **29 pilgrims**, **Tabard Inn**, journey to **Canterbury**.
- **Caedmon** = first English poet; **Alfred** = father of English prose.
- **Bede** wrote his *Ecclesiastical History* in **Latin**.
- **Malory's** *Le Morte d'Arthur* printed by **Caxton (1485)**.
- **Spenser** called Chaucer "**Well of English undefiled**".

ENG-05.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams test irregular comparatives (later/latter, farther/further, elder/older), "superior to" not "than", Latin comparatives, double comparatives, and "one of the + superlative + plural noun".

## Kinds of adjective
| Kind | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Quality (descriptive)** | good, brave, honest, Bangladeshi |
| **Quantity** | much, little, some, enough, whole, all |
| **Number** | one, first, few, many, several, each, every |
| **Demonstrative** | this, that, these, those, such |
| **Interrogative** | which, what, whose (+ noun) |
| **Possessive** | my, your, his, their |
| **Proper** | Bangladeshi, English, Shakespearean |

- **Attributive** use: before the noun ("a **red** rose"). **Predicative** use: after the verb ("The rose is **red**").
- Some adjectives are **only predicative**: **afraid, asleep, alive, alone, awake, aware** ("The child is asleep", not "an asleep child").

## Few / a few / the few, little / a little / the little 🔥
| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **few** (countable) | hardly any (negative) | **Few** men are honest. |
| **a few** | some, a small number (positive) | I have **a few** friends. |
| **the few** | all the (small number) there are | **The few** books he had were lost. |
| **little** (uncountable) | hardly any | There is **little** hope. |
| **a little** | some | There is **a little** milk. |
| **the little** | all the (small amount) there is | **The little** money he had was stolen. |

- **many** + countable; **much** + uncountable. **fewer** + countable (fewer people); **less** + uncountable (less water).

## Degrees of comparison
| Positive | Comparative | Superlative |
|---|---|---|
| tall | taller | tallest |
| beautiful | more beautiful | most beautiful |
| happy | happier | happiest |

### Irregular forms 🔥
| Positive | Comparative | Superlative |
|---|---|---|
| good / well | **better** | **best** |
| bad / ill | **worse** | **worst** |
| much / many | **more** | **most** |
| little | **less / lesser** | **least** |
| **late** | **later** (time) / **latter** (order) | **latest** (time) / **last** (order) |
| **old** | **older** (age, persons or things) / **elder** (family, used before a noun) | **oldest / eldest** |
| **far** | **farther** (distance) / **further** (more, additional) | **farthest / furthest** |
| **near** | nearer | **nearest** (distance) / **next** (order) |
| fore | former | **foremost / first** |

- "My **elder** brother" (not *elder than*); "He is **older than** me."
- "The **latest** news" (newest); "the **last** chapter" (final). "The **latter**" = the second of two.

### Latin comparatives take "to", not "than" 🔥
**superior, inferior, senior, junior, prior, anterior, posterior, major, minor**, and also **prefer, preferable**.
- "He is **senior to** me." — "This cloth is **superior to** that." — "I **prefer** tea **to** coffee."

### Adjectives not compared
**unique, perfect, ideal, complete, round, square, empty, full, excellent, chief, supreme, universal, infinite**. So **not** "more unique", "most perfect".

## Important rules 🔥
1. **No double comparative/superlative**: "more better", "most best" are wrong.
2. **Comparative + than + any other + singular noun** — "Dhaka is **bigger than any other city** in Bangladesh."
3. **One of the + superlative + plural noun + singular verb** — "Rahim **is one of the best boys** in the class." "**One of the students is** absent."
4. **the + comparative …, the + comparative** — "**The more** you read, **the more** you learn."
5. Comparative with **of the two** takes **the** — "Karim is **the taller of the two**."
6. Compare like with like — "The climate of Dhaka is hotter than **that of** Sylhet" (not "than Sylhet").
7. **Superlative with "of all"** — "He is the **best of all**."
8. Positive: **as … as** (affirmative); **so/as … as** (negative) — "He is not **so** tall **as** his brother."

## Order of adjectives
Opinion – size – age – shape – colour – origin – material – purpose + noun: "a **beautiful little old round red Chinese** wooden tea box". Numbers come first: "**the first two** boys" (not "the two first").

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He is more better than me. | He is **better** than I. |
| He is senior than me. | He is **senior to** me. |
| This is the most unique design. | This is a **unique** design. |
| He is elder than me. | He is **older than** I. |
| Dhaka is bigger than any city in Bangladesh. | … than **any other** city … |
| He is one of the best boy. | He is one of the best **boys**. |
| I prefer tea than coffee. | I prefer tea **to** coffee. |
| Less people came. | **Fewer** people came. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **Latin comparatives** (senior, superior, prior, prefer) take **to**.
- 🔥 **farther** = distance, **further** = additional.
- **later/latest** = time; **latter/last** = order.
- **elder** is only for family members and never with "than".
- **Unique, perfect, round** have no degrees.
- "**than any other** + singular noun".
- **few** = hardly any; **a few** = some.

ENG-06.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about *The Faerie Queene* (Gloriana, Redcrosse Knight, Spenserian stanza), Spenser's epithet "Poet's poet", Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus*, "Marlowe's mighty line", and the University Wits.

## The Elizabethan Age (1558–1603)
- Reign of **Queen Elizabeth I**; defeat of the **Spanish Armada (1588)** gave national pride.
- Called the **Golden Age of English literature** (especially drama).
- **Wyatt and Surrey** had brought the **sonnet** into English; their poems appeared in ***Tottel's Miscellany* (1557)**. **Surrey** first used **blank verse** in English (translation of Virgil's *Aeneid*).
- **First English comedy:** ***Ralph Roister Doister*** (Nicholas Udall). **First English tragedy:** ***Gorboduc*** (1561, Sackville and Norton), also the first English play in blank verse.

## Edmund Spenser (c. 1552–1599) 🔥
### Epithets
- **"The Poet's Poet"** — given by **Charles Lamb** 🔥
- **"Prince of poets"** in his own time (the phrase used on his tomb)
- He called Chaucer "**Well of English undefiled**" and saw himself as Chaucer's follower. Buried in **Westminster Abbey** near Chaucer.

### Works
| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Shepheardes Calender*** | **1579** | 12 pastoral eclogues, one for each month; his first major work |
| ***The Faerie Queene*** 🔥 | **1590** (Books I–III), **1596** (IV–VI) | Allegorical epic; planned 12 books, finished **6** (plus the *Mutability Cantos*) |
| ***Amoretti*** | **1595** | Sonnet sequence (88/89 sonnets) to his wife Elizabeth Boyle |
| ***Epithalamion*** | **1595** | Wedding song for his own marriage |
| ***Prothalamion*** | **1596** | Refrain: **"Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song"** |
| *Astrophel* | 1595 | Elegy on Sir Philip Sidney |
| *A View of the Present State of Ireland* | prose | |

### The Faerie Queene 🔥
- The **Faerie Queene = Gloriana**, who represents **Queen Elizabeth I**. The poem is dedicated to her.
- Hero of the whole poem: **Prince Arthur** (Magnificence).
- Each book shows one virtue through a knight:

| Book | Virtue | Knight |
|---|---|---|
| I | **Holiness** | **Redcrosse Knight** (St George), helped by **Una** (truth); enemies **Duessa**, **Archimago** |
| II | Temperance | Sir Guyon |
| III | Chastity | Britomart (a lady knight) |
| IV | Friendship | Cambell and Triamond |
| V | Justice | Artegall |
| VI | Courtesy | Calidore |

- Written in the **Spenserian stanza** 🔥: **9 lines**, 8 lines of iambic pentameter + a final **alexandrine** (iambic hexameter), rhyme **ababbcbcc**. Later used by Byron (*Childe Harold*), Keats (*The Eve of St Agnes*) and Shelley (*Adonais*).
- **Spenserian sonnet** rhyme: abab bcbc cdcd ee (linked quatrains).

## Christopher Marlowe (1564–1593) 🔥
### Epithets and facts
- The greatest of the **University Wits**; born in **Canterbury**, the same year as Shakespeare.
- **"Father of English tragedy"** (common exam answer).
- He made **blank verse** powerful on stage: **Ben Jonson** praised **"Marlowe's mighty line"**.
- Killed in a tavern fight at **Deptford** in **1593**, aged **29**.

### Works
| Work | Approx. year | Main character / fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Tamburlaine the Great*** (Parts 1 and 2) | c. **1587** | A Scythian shepherd who becomes a world conqueror |
| ***Doctor Faustus*** 🔥 | c. **1592** (printed 1604) | Faustus sells his soul to **Lucifer** through **Mephistopheles** for **24 years** of power |
| ***The Jew of Malta*** | c. **1589** | **Barabas**, a greedy, revengeful Jew |
| ***Edward II*** | c. **1592** | History play; the weak king and his favourite **Gaveston** |
| *Dido, Queen of Carthage* | | with Nashe |
| ***Hero and Leander*** | poem | Completed by George Chapman |
| ***"The Passionate Shepherd to His Love"*** | poem | **"Come live with me and be my love"** |

### Famous lines from *Doctor Faustus* 🔥
- **"Was this the face that launched a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?"** (about **Helen of Troy**)
- "Sweet Helen, make me immortal with a kiss."
- "Why this is hell, nor am I out of it." (Mephistopheles)
- Marlowe's heroes show the Renaissance "**overreacher**": unlimited desire for power (Tamburlaine), wealth (Barabas) and knowledge (Faustus).

## The University Wits
Young playwrights educated at **Oxford or Cambridge** who prepared the way for Shakespeare.

| Wit | Famous work |
|---|---|
| **Christopher Marlowe** | *Doctor Faustus* |
| **Thomas Kyd** | ***The Spanish Tragedy*** — model of the **revenge tragedy** |
| **Robert Greene** | *Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay*; called Shakespeare an "**upstart crow**" |
| **John Lyly** | ***Euphues*** (gave us "euphuism", an ornate style) |
| **George Peele** | *The Old Wives' Tale* |
| **Thomas Lodge**, **Thomas Nashe** | *Rosalynde* (source of *As You Like It*); *The Unfortunate Traveller* |

## Other Elizabethans
| Writer | Work / fact |
|---|---|
| **Sir Philip Sidney** | *Arcadia*; *Astrophel and Stella* (sonnets); ***An Apology for Poetry*** (*The Defence of Poesy*) |
| **Francis Bacon** | ***Essays* (1597)** — **"Father of English essay"**; "**Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested**" (*Of Studies*) |
| **Sir Walter Raleigh** | *The History of the World* |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Spenser = **"Poet's poet"** (Charles Lamb).
- 🔥 ***The Faerie Queene***: Gloriana = **Queen Elizabeth**; Book I = **Holiness, Redcrosse Knight**.
- 🔥 **Spenserian stanza**: 9 lines, **ababbcbcc**, last line an **alexandrine**.
- Marlowe: **Doctor Faustus**, **"Marlowe's mighty line"** (Ben Jonson).
- **"Was this the face that launched a thousand ships"** — *Doctor Faustus*, about Helen.
- Kyd's ***The Spanish Tragedy*** = revenge tragedy model.
- **Bacon** = father of the English essay.

ENG-07.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask you to spot a gerund vs a present participle, choose "to + verb" or "verb + ing" after words like *look forward to, avoid, let, make*, and fix dangling participles.

## Finite and non-finite verbs
- A **finite verb** changes with the **subject's person and number and with tense**: "He **goes**." "They **went**." Every complete sentence needs a finite verb.
- A **non-finite verb** does **not** change with the subject or tense: **infinitive, gerund, participle**. "He likes **to swim**." "They like **to swim**."

| Non-finite | Form | Works as |
|---|---|---|
| **Infinitive** | (to) + base verb | noun, adjective, adverb |
| **Gerund** | verb + ing | **noun** |
| **Present participle** | verb + ing | **adjective** (or in continuous tenses) |
| **Past participle** | verb + ed/en | adjective, perfect tenses, passive |

Other verb types: **transitive** (takes an object: "He **wrote** a letter"), **intransitive** (no object: "The baby **sleeps**"), **auxiliary** (be, have, do) and **modal** (can, may, must, shall, will, should, would, might, ought to).

## Infinitive
- **Uses:** subject ("**To err** is human"), object ("I want **to go**"), purpose ("He came **to see** me"), after adjectives ("glad **to meet** you").
- **Bare infinitive (without "to")** 🔥 after:
  - modals: can, could, may, might, must, shall, will, should, would — "You **must go**."
  - **let, make, see, hear, watch, feel, bid, help** (active): "Let him **go**." "He made me **laugh**." "I saw him **cross** the road."
  - **had better, would rather, would sooner, need not, dare not**: "You **had better leave**."
  - But in the **passive**, "to" comes back: "He **was made to work**."
- **Split infinitive** ("to boldly go") is avoided in formal writing: "to go boldly".
- Verbs followed by the infinitive: **want, decide, hope, agree, refuse, promise, plan, wish, expect, afford, pretend, learn**.

## Gerund 🔥
A gerund is **verb + ing used as a noun**.
- Subject: "**Swimming** is good exercise."
- Object: "I enjoy **reading**."
- Object of a preposition: "He is fond of **singing**."
- **A preposition is always followed by a gerund**, never by a bare verb.

### "to" as a preposition + gerund 🔥
**look forward to, with a view to, be used to, be accustomed to, object to, confess to, in addition to, prefer … to, devoted to, given to**:
- "I **look forward to hearing** from you." (not *to hear*)
- "He came **with a view to getting** a job."
- "She **is used to working** late." (compare "He **used to work** late" = past habit).

### Verbs followed by a gerund
**avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, stop, deny, admit, practise, risk, miss, postpone, consider, can't help, it is no use, it is worth, busy**:
- "Would you **mind opening** the window?" — "I **can't help laughing**." — "The book is **worth reading**." — "**It is no use crying** over spilt milk."

### Gerund vs infinitive changes meaning
| Sentence | Meaning |
|---|---|
| He **stopped smoking**. | He gave up smoking. |
| He **stopped to smoke**. | He stopped (walking/work) in order to smoke. |
| I **remember posting** the letter. | I posted it and I remember it. |
| **Remember to post** the letter. | Don't forget to post it. |

### Possessive before a gerund
"I dislike **his** coming late" (not *him coming*). "Excuse **my** being late."

## Participle
- **Present participle** (verb + ing) as adjective: "a **running** train", "**Hearing** the noise, he ran out."
- **Past participle**: "a **broken** chair", "**Written** in haste, the letter had many mistakes."
- **Perfect participle**: "**Having finished** the work, he went home."

### Gerund or participle? 🔥
Ask: does the -ing word name an action (noun) or describe a noun (adjective)?
- "a **walking** stick" = a stick for walking → **gerund** (purpose).
- "a **walking** man" = a man who is walking → **participle**.
- "a **sleeping** baby" → participle; "a **sleeping** car/bag" → gerund.

### Dangling (unrelated) participle 🔥
The participle must refer to the **subject** of the main clause.
- Wrong: "**Walking** along the road, **a snake** bit him." (The snake was not walking.)
- Right: "**Walking** along the road, **he** was bitten by a snake."
- Wrong: "Being a rainy day, I stayed home." Right: "**It being** a rainy day, I stayed home." (**absolute** phrase with its own subject).

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| I look forward to meet you. | I look forward to **meeting** you. |
| He made me to cry. | He made me **cry**. |
| You had better to go now. | You had better **go** now. |
| He is used to get up early. | He is used to **getting** up early. |
| I avoid to eat junk food. | I avoid **eating** junk food. |
| He insisted to go. | He insisted **on going**. |
| Let him to speak. | Let him **speak**. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Finite verb changes with subject/tense; **infinitive, gerund, participle** do not.
- 🔥 **look forward to / with a view to / be used to + -ing**.
- **let, make, see, hear, had better, would rather** + bare infinitive.
- Passive of make: "He **was made to** work."
- **Gerund = noun**, **participle = adjective**.
- **avoid, enjoy, mind, finish, can't help, worth** + gerund.
- A participle must agree with the subject — avoid the dangling participle.

ENG-08.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask which play a character or quotation comes from, the four great tragedies, the tragic flaw of each hero, and basic facts about Shakespeare's life.

## William Shakespeare (1564–1616) 🔥
- Born **23 April 1564** (traditional date; baptised 26 April) at **Stratford-upon-Avon**; died **23 April 1616**.
- Wife: **Anne Hathaway**. Son **Hamnet** died young.
- Wrote about **37 plays** (some count 38 or 39 with collaborations), **154 sonnets** and two long poems (***Venus and Adonis***, ***The Rape of Lucrece***).
- Theatre company: **Lord Chamberlain's Men**, later the **King's Men**; theatre: **The Globe** (1599).
- First collected edition: the **First Folio (1623)**, by his fellow actors **John Heminges and Henry Condell**; it has **36 plays**.
- Epithets: **"The Bard of Avon"**, **"Swan of Avon"** (Ben Jonson), "the national poet of England". Ben Jonson wrote that he was "**not of an age, but for all time**".

## The four great tragedies 🔥🔥
| Play | Approx. date | Hero & tragic flaw | Setting |
|---|---|---|---|
| ***Hamlet*** | c. **1600–01** | Prince of Denmark; **indecision / delay** | Denmark (Elsinore) |
| ***Othello*** | c. **1603–04** | The Moor of Venice; **jealousy** | Venice, Cyprus |
| ***King Lear*** | c. **1605–06** | Old king of Britain; **pride and poor judgement** | Britain |
| ***Macbeth*** | c. **1606** | Scottish general; **ambition** | Scotland |

**Memory hook:** *HOLM — Hamlet, Othello, Lear, Macbeth.* ***Macbeth* is the shortest** tragedy; ***Hamlet* is the longest** play.

## Characters and famous lines
### Hamlet
- Characters: **Hamlet**, his father's **Ghost**, uncle **Claudius** (murderer, now king), mother **Gertrude**, **Polonius**, his daughter **Ophelia** (Hamlet's love), son **Laertes**, friend **Horatio**, **Rosencrantz and Guildenstern**, **Yorick** (the dead jester's skull).
- Lines: 🔥 **"To be, or not to be: that is the question."** — **"Frailty, thy name is woman!"** — "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark." — "Brevity is the soul of wit." (Polonius) — "Neither a borrower nor a lender be." (Polonius) — "Alas, poor Yorick!" — "The rest is silence." — "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio…"
- Play-within-a-play: ***The Mousetrap*** (The Murder of Gonzago).

### Othello
- **Othello** (black general), wife **Desdemona**, villain **Iago** (his ensign), **Cassio** (lieutenant), **Emilia** (Iago's wife), **Roderigo**, Desdemona's father **Brabantio**. The **handkerchief** is the "proof".
- Lines: **"O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-eyed monster…"** (Iago) — "one that loved not wisely but too well" (Othello).

### King Lear
- **Lear** divides his kingdom among daughters **Goneril, Regan** (flatterers) and **Cordelia** (honest, disowned). Subplot: **Gloucester** and his sons **Edgar** (loyal) and **Edmund** (bastard, villain). **The Fool**; **Kent**.
- Lines: "Nothing will come of nothing." — "How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is / To have a thankless child!" — "I am a man more sinned against than sinning." — "As flies to wanton boys are we to the gods; / They kill us for their sport." (Gloucester)

### Macbeth
- **Macbeth**, **Lady Macbeth**, **King Duncan** (murdered), **Banquo** (his ghost appears), **Macduff** (kills Macbeth; "from his mother's womb untimely ripped"), **Malcolm**, **the three Witches**.
- Lines: **"Fair is foul, and foul is fair."** (Witches) — **"Out, damned spot!"** (Lady Macbeth, sleepwalking) — "Is this a dagger which I see before me?" — 🔥 **"Life's but a walking shadow… a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing."** — "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow." — "All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand."
- Called "**the Scottish play**" by superstitious actors.

## Other tragedies
| Play | Key fact / line |
|---|---|
| ***Romeo and Juliet*** (c. 1595) | Lovers from the **Montague** and **Capulet** families of **Verona**; "**What's in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet**"; "star-cross'd lovers" |
| ***Julius Caesar*** (1599) | **Brutus**, Cassius, **Mark Antony**; "**Et tu, Brute?**"; "**Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears**"; "Beware the Ides of March"; "Cowards die many times before their deaths" |
| ***Antony and Cleopatra*** | Roman general and Egyptian queen |
| *Titus Andronicus* | His earliest, bloody revenge tragedy |
| *Timon of Athens*, *Coriolanus* | Roman/Greek tragedies |

- **"The noblest Roman of them all"** — Antony about **Brutus**.
- A. C. Bradley's ***Shakespearean Tragedy* (1904)** is the classic study of the four great tragedies.

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Four great tragedies: **Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth**.
- 🔥 "To be, or not to be" — **Hamlet**; "Frailty, thy name is woman" — **Hamlet**.
- 🔥 "Green-eyed monster" — **Othello** (spoken by Iago).
- "Out, damned spot" — **Lady Macbeth**; "Fair is foul" — the **Witches**.
- Cordelia = Lear's honest daughter; Desdemona = Othello's wife.
- "Et tu, Brute?" — ***Julius Caesar***.
- Shakespeare: **154 sonnets**, about **37 plays**, **First Folio 1623**.

ENG-09.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Tense questions fill "right form of verb" and error-detection items: "since/for", "no sooner … than", "it is time + past", present tense after "if/when" for the future, and verbs never used in continuous forms.

## The 12 tenses 🔥
| Tense | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Present** | He **writes** | He **is writing** | He **has written** | He **has been writing** |
| **Past** | He **wrote** | He **was writing** | He **had written** | He **had been writing** |
| **Future** | He **will write** | He **will be writing** | He **will have written** | He **will have been writing** |

## Present tenses
**Present indefinite (simple)** — habits, general and universal truths, timetables:
- "The sun **rises** in the east." "Honesty **is** the best policy." "The train **leaves** at 6 pm."
- Signal words: always, usually, often, every day, daily, generally.
- After **if, when, until, unless, as soon as, before, after** in a future sense 🔥: "I will wait **until** he **comes**" (not *will come*). "**If** it **rains**, we will stay home."
- Headlines and **vivid narration**: "Now the hero **enters**."

**Present continuous** — action now or a fixed future plan: "Look! It **is raining**." "I **am leaving** tomorrow."
- 🔥 **Stative verbs are not used in continuous forms**: **know, understand, believe, like, love, hate, want, wish, see, hear, smell, taste, seem, belong, own, possess, contain, remember, prefer**. "I **know** him" (not *am knowing*). "I **see** a bird" (not *am seeing*).

**Present perfect** — past action with present result, or with just/already/yet/ever/never/recently/lately/so far:
- "I **have** just **finished** the work."
- 🔥 **Never with a definite past time** (yesterday, last year, ago, in 2020): "I **saw** him yesterday" (not *have seen*).

**Present perfect continuous** — action began in the past and is still going on, with **since / for**:
- "He **has been reading** **since** morning." "It **has been raining for** two hours."
- **since** + point of time (since 2010, since Monday); **for** + period (for two years).

## Past tenses
- **Past indefinite:** yesterday, ago, last, in 1971: "Bangladesh **became** independent **in 1971**."
- **Past continuous:** "I **was reading** when he **came**." (long action interrupted by a short one)
- **Past perfect:** of two past actions, the **earlier** one is past perfect 🔥: "The patient **had died before** the doctor **came**." "The train **had left** before we **reached** the station."

## Future tenses
- **shall** with I/we, **will** with others (traditional rule); modern English uses **will** for all. For determination/promise the rule reverses: "You **shall** be punished."
- **Future perfect:** "By next June I **will have finished** the course." (with **by** + future time)
- **be going to** for plans and signs: "It **is going to** rain."

## Special structures 🔥
| Structure | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **It is time / It is high time** | + subject + **past** verb | "It is high time we **left**." |
| **No sooner … than** | **had + subject + V3 … than + past** | "**No sooner had** he **reached** the station **than** the train **left**." |
| **Hardly / Scarcely … when/before** | **had + subject + V3 … when + past** | "**Hardly had** I **gone** out **when** it began to rain." |
| **Since** (conjunction) | main clause present perfect + since + past simple | "It **has been** ten years **since** he **died**." |
| **Wish** (unreal present) | + past (be → **were**) | "I wish I **were** a bird." "I wish I **knew** the answer." |
| **As if / as though** | + past; be → **were** | "He talks **as if** he **were** a king." |
| **Would rather** (present) | + subject + past | "I would rather you **went** now." |
| **Before** after a negative | "**It was not long before** he **came**." | |

- **Sequence of tenses:** a past main verb is followed by a past verb in the clause: "He said that he **was** ill." Exception — universal truth: "He said that the earth **moves** round the sun."
- **lest … should**: "Walk fast **lest** you **should** miss the train."

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| I am knowing him for years. | I **have known** him for years. |
| I have seen him yesterday. | I **saw** him yesterday. |
| He is ill since Monday. | He **has been** ill since Monday. |
| I will wait till he will come. | I will wait till he **comes**. |
| It is time we go home. | It is time we **went** home. |
| No sooner did he come when it rained. | No sooner **had he come than** it rained. |
| He has been living here since two years. | … **for** two years. |
| He said that he is busy. | He said that he **was** busy. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **since** + point of time; **for** + period.
- 🔥 **No sooner had … than**; **Hardly/Scarcely had … when**.
- 🔥 **It is (high) time + past**.
- Present perfect is **never** used with yesterday/ago/last.
- Earlier of two past actions → **past perfect**.
- Future after **if/when/until** → **present simple**.
- **know, like, see, belong** are not used in continuous tenses.
- Universal truths stay in the **present** in reported speech.

ENG-10.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask which play a character belongs to (Shylock, Portia, Prospero, Falstaff, Puck), the classification of plays, famous comic lines, and facts about the 154 sonnets (Fair Youth, Dark Lady, Sonnet 18).

## How Shakespeare's plays are grouped
The **First Folio (1623)** divided the plays into **Comedies, Histories and Tragedies**. Critics later added **Romances (late plays)** and **Problem plays**.

## Comedies 🔥
| Play | Approx. date | Key characters / facts |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Comedy of Errors*** | c. 1592–94 | Two sets of identical twins; **shortest play** |
| ***The Taming of the Shrew*** | c. 1590–92 | **Petruchio** tames **Katherina** |
| ***A Midsummer Night's Dream*** 🔥 | c. **1595–96** | Fairies **Oberon, Titania, Puck**; **Bottom** (gets an ass's head); lovers in a wood near **Athens**. "**The course of true love never did run smooth.**" "Lord, what fools these mortals be!" (Puck) |
| ***The Merchant of Venice*** 🔥 | c. **1596–97** | **Shylock** (Jewish moneylender) demands a **pound of flesh** from **Antonio**; **Portia** disguised as a lawyer; **Bassanio**, **Jessica**. "**The quality of mercy is not strained**" (Portia). "All that glisters is not gold." |
| ***Much Ado About Nothing*** | c. 1598–99 | **Beatrice and Benedick**; **Dogberry** |
| ***As You Like It*** 🔥 | c. **1599** | **Rosalind** (disguised as Ganymede), **Orlando**, **Jaques**, the Forest of **Arden**. "**All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players**" — the **seven ages of man** speech (Jaques) |
| ***Twelfth Night*** | c. **1601** | **Viola** (disguised as Cesario), **Orsino**, **Olivia**, **Malvolio**. "**If music be the food of love, play on**" (opening line). "Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em." |
| ***The Merry Wives of Windsor*** | c. 1597–1601 | **Falstaff** in love-plots |

- **Mature / joyous comedies:** *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, *The Merchant of Venice*, *Much Ado*, *As You Like It*, *Twelfth Night*.
- **Problem plays / dark comedies:** ***Measure for Measure***, ***All's Well That Ends Well***, ***Troilus and Cressida***.

## Romances (last plays)
| Play | Fact |
|---|---|
| ***The Tempest*** 🔥 (c. **1610–11**) | Usually considered his **last complete play** written alone. **Prospero** (magician, Duke of Milan), daughter **Miranda**, spirit **Ariel**, monster **Caliban**, **Ferdinand**. "**O brave new world, / That has such people in't!**" (Miranda). "We are such stuff / As dreams are made on." |
| ***The Winter's Tale*** | **Leontes**, **Hermione**, **Perdita**; stage direction "**Exit, pursued by a bear**" |
| ***Cymbeline***, ***Pericles*** | Romances of loss and reunion |

## History plays 🔥
Ten plays on English kings, mainly from **Holinshed's *Chronicles***.

| Play | Key fact |
|---|---|
| ***Henry VI*** (Parts 1–3) | His early plays; Wars of the Roses |
| ***Richard III*** | Villain-king; "**Now is the winter of our discontent**"; "**A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!**" |
| ***Richard II*** | "This royal throne of kings, this sceptred isle… **this England**" (John of Gaunt) |
| ***Henry IV*** (Parts 1–2) | **Sir John Falstaff** (the fat comic knight), **Prince Hal**, **Hotspur**. "**Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown**" |
| ***Henry V*** | Battle of **Agincourt**; "**Once more unto the breach, dear friends**"; "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers" |
| ***King John***, ***Henry VIII*** | *Henry VIII* was written with **John Fletcher**; a cannon fired during it burned down **the Globe (1613)** |

- **Falstaff** is Shakespeare's most famous comic character (in *Henry IV* and *The Merry Wives of Windsor*).

## Sonnets 🔥
- **154 sonnets**, published in **1609** (by Thomas Thorpe), dedicated to the mysterious "**Mr. W. H.**".
- **Sonnets 1–126:** to the **Fair Youth** (a young man); **127–152:** to the **Dark Lady**; a **Rival Poet** also appears.
- **Shakespearean (English) sonnet:** **three quatrains + a couplet**, rhyme **abab cdcd efef gg**, in iambic pentameter.
- Famous sonnets:
  - **Sonnet 18:** "**Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?**"
  - **Sonnet 116:** "**Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments.**"
  - **Sonnet 130:** "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun."
  - **Sonnet 29:** "When, in disgrace with fortune and men's eyes."
- **Long poems:** ***Venus and Adonis*** (1593), ***The Rape of Lucrece*** (1594), both dedicated to the **Earl of Southampton**.

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **Shylock, Portia, Antonio** — *The Merchant of Venice*.
- 🔥 **"All the world's a stage"** — *As You Like It* (Jaques).
- 🔥 **Prospero, Miranda, Ariel, Caliban** — *The Tempest*.
- **Puck, Oberon, Bottom** — *A Midsummer Night's Dream*.
- **Falstaff** — *Henry IV* and *The Merry Wives of Windsor*.
- "If music be the food of love" — *Twelfth Night*.
- **154 sonnets**, 1609; Sonnet 18 = "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?"
- Shakespearean sonnet rhyme: **abab cdcd efef gg**.

ENG-11.notes:
> **Why it matters:** This is the single most tested grammar area in error detection: "one of the …", "each/every", "either … or", "as well as", "a number of / the number of", and collective nouns.

## Basic rule
A **singular subject takes a singular verb**, and a **plural subject takes a plural verb**. "He **writes**." "They **write**." Find the real subject and ignore words between the subject and the verb:
- "**The quality** of the mangoes **is** good." (not *are*)
- "**The leader**, with all his followers, **was** arrested."

## Rules exams love 🔥
| # | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Two subjects joined by **and** → plural | "Rahim **and** Karim **are** friends." |
| 2 | **and** but one person/thing or one idea → singular | "**The poet and philosopher is** dead." (one person) "**Bread and butter is** my breakfast." "**Slow and steady wins** the race." |
| 3 | **each / every** + noun joined by and → singular | "**Every** boy and girl **was** present." "**Each** man and woman **has** a vote." |
| 4 | **as well as, with, along with, together with, besides, in addition to, like, including, accompanied by** → verb agrees with the **first** subject | "The captain, **as well as** the players, **was** happy." |
| 5 | **either … or / neither … nor / or / nor / not only … but also** → verb agrees with the **nearer** subject | "Neither the teacher nor **the students were** present." "Either you or **he is** wrong." |
| 6 | **one of the + plural noun + singular verb** 🔥 | "**One of the boys is** absent." |
| 7 | **one of the + plural noun + who/that + plural verb** | "He is one of **the best players who have** played for Bangladesh." |
| 8 | **each, every, everyone, everybody, anyone, someone, no one, nobody, nothing, either, neither** → singular | "**Everyone is** here." "**Neither** of the answers **is** correct." |
| 9 | **A number of** + plural noun → **plural** | "**A number of** students **were** absent." |
| 10 | **The number of** + plural noun → **singular** | "**The number of** students **is** increasing." |
| 11 | **many a** + singular noun → **singular** | "**Many a man has** fallen." |
| 12 | **More than one** + singular noun → singular | "**More than one** student **was** punished." |
| 13 | **Collective noun** as a unit → singular; as individuals → plural | "The **jury has** given its verdict." "The **jury are** divided in their opinions." |
| 14 | Always-plural nouns → plural | "The **police are** coming." "**Cattle are** grazing." "My **scissors are** blunt." |
| 15 | Plural-looking singulars → singular | "**Mathematics is** easy." "**The news is** true." |
| 16 | Amount, distance, time, money as one sum → singular | "**Ten miles is** a long way." "**Five thousand taka is** enough." "**Two years is** a long time." |
| 17 | Title of a book / country name → singular | "***Gulliver's Travels* is** a satire." "**The United States is** rich." |
| 18 | **The + adjective** (people) → plural | "**The rich are** not always happy." "**The poor need** help." |
| 19 | **None / all / some / most / half / part of + noun** → agrees with the noun after "of" | "**Some of the milk is** sour." "**Some of the boys are** late." "**Half of the money was** spent." |
| 20 | **There / Here** + verb + subject → verb agrees with what follows | "**There is** a book." "**There are** many books." |
| 21 | Relative pronoun → verb agrees with the antecedent | "It is **I who am** responsible." |
| 22 | **Not only X but also Y** → agrees with Y | "Not only the students but also **the teacher was** there." |

## Tricky subjects
- **Gerund / infinitive / clause** as subject → singular: "**Walking** in the morning **is** good." "**What he says is** true."
- **Percentage / fraction** + uncountable → singular; + plural noun → plural: "**Sixty percent of the land is** fertile." "**Sixty percent of the voters were** women."
- **a pair of** → singular: "**A pair of** shoes **is** under the bed." but "My **trousers are** torn."
- **The majority** → plural if people are meant: "**The majority** of students **are** girls."

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| One of my friends are a doctor. | One of my friends **is** a doctor. |
| The number of cars are increasing. | The number of cars **is** increasing. |
| A number of students was absent. | A number of students **were** absent. |
| Each of the boys have a book. | Each of the boys **has** a book. |
| The teacher, as well as the students, were present. | … **was** present. |
| Neither he nor I are guilty. | Neither he nor I **am** guilty. |
| Many a student have failed. | Many a student **has** failed. |
| The news are good. | The news **is** good. |
| The police has caught the thief. | The police **have** caught the thief. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **One of the + plural noun + singular verb**.
- 🔥 **A number of** → plural; **the number of** → singular.
- 🔥 **as well as / with / along with** → verb follows the **first** subject.
- **either/neither … or/nor** → verb follows the **nearer** subject.
- **each, every, many a, more than one** → singular.
- **The rich, the poor, police, cattle, people** → plural.
- **news, mathematics, ten miles, five thousand taka** → singular.

ENG-12.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about Jonson's comedy of humours (*Volpone*), the term "metaphysical poets" (who coined it), Donne's famous lines, and Milton's epics (*Paradise Lost*, number of books, Satan, "to justify the ways of God to men").

## Ben Jonson (1572–1637)
- Friend and rival of Shakespeare; the **first Poet Laureate** in practice (royal pension, 1616) — the first *official* Poet Laureate was **Dryden (1668)**.
- Father of the **Comedy of Humours** 🔥 (characters dominated by one "humour" or trait).
- Leader of the "**Tribe of Ben**" / "**Sons of Ben**" (Cavalier poets like Herrick followed him).
- Wrote **masques** for the court.
- Tribute to Shakespeare: "**Sweet Swan of Avon**", "**He was not of an age, but for all time!**"

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Every Man in His Humour*** | **1598** | Shakespeare acted in it; first comedy of humours |
| ***Volpone*** (*The Fox*) 🔥 | **1605/06** | Greedy Venetian **Volpone** and his servant **Mosca** (the fly) |
| ***The Alchemist*** | **1610** | Subtle, Face, Dol Common |
| ***Bartholomew Fair*** | 1614 | |
| ***Epicoene, or The Silent Woman*** | 1609 | |
| Poems | | "**Drink to me only with thine eyes**" (*Song: To Celia*); "On My First Son" |
| *Timber, or Discoveries* | prose | Critical notes |

## Metaphysical poetry 🔥
- The term was used by **Dryden** (Donne "affects the metaphysics") and made popular by **Dr. Samuel Johnson** in his ***Life of Cowley*** (*Lives of the Poets*). Johnson is usually credited with coining "metaphysical poets".
- Features: **wit**, **conceits** (far-fetched comparisons), argument, colloquial openings, learned images from science and philosophy.
- Johnson's criticism: "**The most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together.**"
- **T. S. Eliot** revived them (essay "The Metaphysical Poets", 1921; "**dissociation of sensibility**").
- Poets: **John Donne** (leader), **George Herbert**, **Andrew Marvell**, **Henry Vaughan**, **Richard Crashaw**, **Abraham Cowley**.

## John Donne (1572–1631) 🔥
- **Father / leader of metaphysical poetry**. Became **Dean of St Paul's Cathedral** (1621).

| Work | Fact / famous line |
|---|---|
| ***Songs and Sonnets*** (pub. 1633) | Love poems |
| "**The Canonization**" | "**For God's sake hold your tongue, and let me love**" |
| "**The Sun Rising**" | "**Busy old fool, unruly sun**" |
| "**A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning**" | Famous **compass conceit** (lovers as the two legs of a compass) |
| "**The Flea**" | Lovers' blood mixed in a flea |
| "**Go and catch a falling star**" (*Song*) | |
| ***Holy Sonnets*** | "**Death, be not proud**" (Holy Sonnet 10); "**Batter my heart, three-person'd God**" |
| ***Devotions upon Emergent Occasions*** (1624, prose) | 🔥 "**No man is an island**" and "**never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee**" |

Other metaphysicals: **Marvell** — "**To His Coy Mistress**" ("Had we but world enough, and time"); **Herbert** — *The Temple* ("The Collar", "Virtue"); **Vaughan** — *Silex Scintillans* ("The Retreat").

## John Milton (1608–1674) 🔥🔥
- Puritan poet; secretary (Latin Secretary) to **Oliver Cromwell's** government.
- Became **totally blind by 1652**; he **dictated *Paradise Lost***.
- Epithets: "**The organ voice of England**" (Tennyson called him "God-gifted organ-voice of England"); the **"Epic poet of England"**; Wordsworth: "**Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour**" (sonnet *London, 1802*).

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***On the Morning of Christ's Nativity*** | 1629 | Early ode |
| ***L'Allegro*** and ***Il Penseroso*** | c. 1631 | Twin poems: the cheerful man and the thoughtful man |
| ***Comus*** | 1634 | A masque |
| ***Lycidas*** 🔥 | **1637** | **Pastoral elegy** on his friend **Edward King**, drowned at sea |
| ***Areopagitica*** 🔥 | **1644** | Prose; defence of **freedom of the press**: "**A good book is the precious life-blood of a master spirit**" |
| ***Paradise Lost*** 🔥 | **1667** (10 books); **1674** (**12 books**) | Epic in **blank verse** on the Fall of Man |
| ***Paradise Regained*** | **1671** | 4 books; Christ resists Satan's temptation |
| ***Samson Agonistes*** | **1671** | Closet tragedy on the Greek model |
| Sonnet "**On His Blindness**" | c. 1652–55 | "**They also serve who only stand and wait.**" |

### Paradise Lost 🔥
- Theme: **the Fall of Man** — **Adam and Eve** disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit; **Satan** (tempts Eve in the form of a **serpent**).
- Aim: "**to justify the ways of God to men**" (Book I).
- Opening: "**Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree…**"
- Satan's lines: "**Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heaven.**" — "**The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.**"
- Satan is often called the **real hero** (Blake: Milton was "of the Devil's party without knowing it").
- **Pandemonium** — capital of Hell (Milton coined the word).
- Written in **blank verse** (unrhymed iambic pentameter); style is called the **"grand style"**.

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Ben Jonson: **comedy of humours**, ***Volpone***, *The Alchemist*.
- 🔥 **Dr. Johnson** named the metaphysical poets (in *Life of Cowley*).
- 🔥 Donne: **father of metaphysical poetry**; "**No man is an island**"; "**Death, be not proud**".
- Compass conceit — "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning".
- 🔥 *Paradise Lost*: **12 books** (1674 edition), **blank verse**, "to justify the ways of God to men".
- "They also serve who only stand and wait" — **On His Blindness**.
- ***Lycidas*** = pastoral elegy; ***Areopagitica*** = freedom of the press.

ENG-13.notes:
> **Why it matters:** "Right form of verbs" items test fixed structures: "as if + were", "It is time + past", "would rather", "lest … should", "no sooner … than", conditionals, and verbs after modals and prepositions.

## Step-by-step method
1. Find the **subject** (singular/plural, person).
2. Look for **time words** (yesterday, since, for, already, tomorrow).
3. Check for **fixed structures** (below).
4. Check whether the verb is after a **modal**, a **preposition** or **"to"**.

## Fixed structures 🔥
| Structure | Verb form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **as if / as though** (unreal) | past; be → **were** for all subjects | "He behaves **as if** he **were** a king." "She talks as if she **knew** everything." |
| **I wish / If only** (present) | past; be → **were** | "I wish I **were** rich." |
| **wish** (past) | had + V3 | "I wish I **had studied** harder." |
| **It is time / high time / about time** | subject + **past** | "It is high time we **changed** the system." |
| **It is time** + to-infinitive | | "It is time **to go**." |
| **would rather / would sooner** + subject | past | "I'd rather you **stayed** here." |
| **would rather** (same subject) | bare verb | "I **would rather die** than beg." |
| **had better** | bare verb | "You **had better take** rest." |
| **lest** | **should** + bare verb | "Work hard **lest** you **should fail**." |
| **No sooner … than** | had + subject + V3 … than + past | "No sooner **had** the bell **rung** than the students **left**." |
| **Hardly / Scarcely … when/before** | had + subject + V3 … when + past | "Scarcely **had** he **arrived** when it **started** to rain." |
| **Since** (time) | present perfect + since + past | "Ten years **have passed** since he **left**." |
| **Suggest / propose / insist / demand / recommend that** | subject + (should) + **bare verb** (subjunctive) | "The doctor suggested that he **(should) take** rest." "I insist that he **be** present." |
| **May** (wish) | may + subject + bare verb | "**May** you **live** long!" |
| **Let** | object + bare verb | "Let him **go**." |
| **would that** | past | "Would that I **were** young again!" |

## Conditional sentences 🔥
| Type | If-clause | Main clause | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** (fact) | present | present | "If you heat ice, it **melts**." |
| **1** (possible) | **present** | **will** + V1 | "If it **rains**, I **will stay** home." |
| **2** (unreal present) | **past** (were) | **would** + V1 | "If I **were** a bird, I **would fly**." |
| **3** (unreal past) | **had + V3** | **would have** + V3 | "If he **had worked** hard, he **would have passed**." |

- Inversion: "**Had** I **known**, I would have helped." "**Were** I you, I would accept." "**Should** it rain, stay home."
- **Unless** = if not; do not add another "not": "Unless you **work** hard, you will fail."

## Verbs after modals, prepositions and "to"
- **Modal + bare verb:** "He can **swim**." "You must **go**." "He ought **to go**" (ought takes *to*).
- **Preposition + gerund:** "He is fond **of swimming**." "He left **without saying** goodbye." "He insisted **on going**."
- **"to" as preposition + gerund:** look forward to, with a view to, be used to, be accustomed to, object to: "I am used **to walking**."
- **used to + V1** (past habit): "I **used to walk** daily."
- **make / let / see / hear + object + bare verb** (active); **was made to + V1** (passive).
- **need / dare** as modals (negative/question): "You **need not go**." "How **dare** he **enter**?"
- **Causative:** **have / get something done**: "I **had** my hair **cut**." "Get the letter **typed**."

## Subject-verb and tense clues
| Clue | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| every day, always, usually | present simple | "He **goes** to school every day." |
| now, at present, look!, listen! | present continuous | "Look! The baby **is sleeping**." |
| just, already, yet, ever, recently | present perfect | "I have just **finished**." |
| since / for (still going on) | present perfect (continuous) | "He **has been living** here since 2015." |
| yesterday, ago, last, in 2010 | past simple | "He **came** yesterday." |
| before / after two past actions | earlier one past perfect | "He **had left** before I came." |
| tomorrow, next week | future | "He **will come** tomorrow." |
| by + future time | future perfect | "By 2030 I **will have retired**." |
| universal truth | present | "The sun **rises** in the east." |

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He talks as if he was a leader. | … as if he **were** a leader. |
| It is time we start. | It is time we **started**. |
| Walk carefully lest you fall down. (exam style) | … lest you **should fall** down. |
| If I was you, I would go. | If I **were** you, I would go. |
| If he had come, I would help him. | … I **would have helped** him. |
| I am used to get up early. | I am used to **getting** up early. |
| He suggested me to go. | He suggested that I **(should) go**. |
| He can sings. | He can **sing**. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **as if / wish + were** (for every subject).
- 🔥 **It is (high) time + past**.
- 🔥 **lest + should + V1**.
- **would rather + subject + past**; **had better + V1**.
- Conditional 3: **had + V3 → would have + V3**.
- **suggest/insist/demand that + (should) + V1**.
- Preposition + **-ing**.

ENG-14.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about the first Poet Laureate (Dryden), Pope's mock-epic *The Rape of the Lock*, Swift's *Gulliver's Travels* (Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Houyhnhnms), *Robinson Crusoe* (first English novel), and famous lines like "To err is human".

## Background
- **Restoration (1660):** Charles II returns; theatres reopen; women act on stage for the first time.
- **Neo-classical / Augustan Age (1700–1745):** writers imitate Greek and Roman models; value **reason, order, wit, correctness**; favourite form is the **heroic couplet**; favourite mode is **satire**.
- **Comedy of manners** (Restoration comedy): **William Congreve** — ***The Way of the World*** (1700), *Love for Love*; **Wycherley** — *The Country Wife*.
- **John Bunyan** — ***The Pilgrim's Progress*** (1678), allegory; hero **Christian** travels from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City.
- **Periodical essay:** **Richard Steele** — ***The Tatler*** (1709); **Joseph Addison and Steele** — ***The Spectator*** (1711), with **Sir Roger de Coverley**.

## John Dryden (1631–1700) 🔥
- **First official Poet Laureate of England (1668)**.
- Epithets: **"Father of English criticism"** (Dr. Johnson), dominant figure of the **Age of Dryden**.
- He called Chaucer the "**Father of English poetry**" and said of *The Canterbury Tales*: "**Here is God's plenty**."

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Absalom and Achitophel*** 🔥 | **1681** | Political **satire** in heroic couplets (Achitophel = Earl of Shaftesbury) |
| ***MacFlecknoe*** | 1682 | Mock-heroic satire on the poet **Shadwell** |
| ***An Essay of Dramatic Poesy*** | **1668** | Critical dialogue (Neander = Dryden) |
| ***All for Love*** | **1677** | Tragedy on **Antony and Cleopatra** in blank verse |
| *Annus Mirabilis* | 1667 | "Year of wonders" (1666: war and Great Fire) |
| *The Hind and the Panther* | 1687 | Religious allegory |
| *Alexander's Feast* | 1697 | Ode |

## Alexander Pope (1688–1744) 🔥
- Greatest poet of the Augustan age (**Age of Pope**); master of the **heroic couplet**; a Catholic, physically small and ill.
- Translated Homer's ***Iliad*** and ***Odyssey***.

| Work | Year | Fact / famous line |
|---|---|---|
| ***An Essay on Criticism*** | **1711** | 🔥 "**To err is human, to forgive divine.**" — "**A little learning is a dangerous thing.**" — "**Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.**" |
| ***The Rape of the Lock*** 🔥 | **1712/1714** | **Mock-epic**; Lord Petre cuts a lock of **Belinda's** (Arabella Fermor's) hair |
| ***The Dunciad*** | 1728 | Mock-epic satire on dull writers ("dunces") |
| ***An Essay on Man*** | **1733–34** | 🔥 "**The proper study of mankind is Man.**" — "**Hope springs eternal in the human breast.**" — "Whatever is, is right." |
| *Epistle to Dr Arbuthnot* | 1735 | Satire on **Addison** as "Atticus" |
| *Ode on Solitude* | | "Happy the man whose wish and care / A few paternal acres bound" |

## Jonathan Swift (1667–1745) 🔥
- Irish (Anglo-Irish) satirist; **Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin**.
- The **greatest prose satirist** in English.

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Gulliver's Travels*** 🔥 | **1726** | Satire on mankind; hero **Lemuel Gulliver**, a ship's surgeon |
| ***A Tale of a Tub*** | 1704 | Satire on religious corruption |
| ***The Battle of the Books*** | 1704 | Ancients vs Moderns ("**sweetness and light**" — bee's image; later used by Arnold) |
| ***A Modest Proposal*** | **1729** | Ironic proposal that the poor Irish sell their babies as food |
| *Journal to Stella* | | Letters to Esther Johnson ("Stella") |

### Gulliver's four voyages 🔥
| Part | Land | People |
|---|---|---|
| I | **Lilliput** | Tiny people (**6 inches**); Lilliput vs **Blefuscu**; Big-Endians and Little-Endians |
| II | **Brobdingnag** | **Giants** |
| III | **Laputa** (flying island), Balnibarbi, Glubbdubdrib, Luggnagg | Impractical scientists; the immortal **Struldbrugs** |
| IV | **Land of the Houyhnhnms** | Rational **horses (Houyhnhnms)**; brutish human-like **Yahoos** |

## Daniel Defoe (c. 1660–1731) 🔥
- Journalist and novelist; some books call him the "Father of the English novel", but most exam guides give that title to **Henry Fielding** (see the 18th-century novel note).
- ***Robinson Crusoe*** (**1719**) is often called the **first English novel** 🔥. Crusoe is shipwrecked on an island for **28 years**; his servant is **Friday**. Based partly on the real sailor **Alexander Selkirk**.

| Work | Year |
|---|---|
| ***Robinson Crusoe*** | **1719** |
| *Captain Singleton* | 1720 |
| ***Moll Flanders*** | **1722** |
| ***A Journal of the Plague Year*** | 1722 |
| *Roxana* | 1724 |
| *The Shortest Way with the Dissenters* | 1702 (satire; he was pilloried) |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **Dryden** = first Poet Laureate (1668), "Father of English criticism".
- 🔥 ***The Rape of the Lock*** (Pope) = mock-epic; heroine **Belinda**.
- 🔥 "**To err is human, to forgive divine**" and "**A little learning is a dangerous thing**" — Pope, *An Essay on Criticism*.
- 🔥 ***Gulliver's Travels* (1726)**: **Lilliput** (tiny), **Brobdingnag** (giants), **Houyhnhnms** (horses), **Yahoos**.
- ***Robinson Crusoe* (1719)** — Defoe; servant **Friday**.
- *The Pilgrim's Progress* — **Bunyan**; *The Way of the World* — **Congreve**.
- *The Spectator* — **Addison & Steele**.

ENG-15.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams test adjective vs adverb confusion (good/well, hard/hardly, late/lately), the position of "only", "enough", "too … to", "very/much", and inversion after negative adverbs ("Never have I seen").

## What an adverb does
An **adverb** modifies a **verb, an adjective, another adverb** or a whole sentence.
- "He runs **fast**." (verb) — "She is **very** beautiful." (adjective) — "He spoke **quite** clearly." (adverb) — "**Fortunately**, nobody was hurt." (sentence)

## Kinds of adverb
| Kind | Answers | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | when? | now, then, today, soon, already, yet, ago, lately |
| **Place** | where? | here, there, everywhere, inside, above |
| **Manner** | how? | quickly, slowly, well, bravely, carefully |
| **Frequency** | how often? | always, often, never, seldom, rarely, sometimes, once |
| **Degree / quantity** | how much? | very, too, quite, almost, enough, fully, rather |
| **Affirmation / negation** | | yes, certainly, surely, no, not, never |
| **Reason** | why? | therefore, hence, so |
| **Interrogative** | | when? where? how? why? |
| **Relative** | joins clauses | "This is the place **where** he was born." |

## Adjective or adverb? 🔥
| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **hard** | with effort | "He works **hard**." |
| **hardly** | scarcely, almost not | "He **hardly** works." (= he does little work) |
| **late** | not on time | "He came **late**." |
| **lately** | recently | "I have not seen him **lately**." |
| **near** | close by | "He lives **near**." |
| **nearly** | almost | "I **nearly** missed the bus." |
| **high / highly** | height / very much | "The kite flew **high**." "He is **highly** educated." |
| **most / mostly** | superlative / mainly | "The guests were **mostly** students." |
| **good** (adj) / **well** (adv) | | "He is a **good** singer; he sings **well**." "I am **well**" (healthy — here *well* is an adjective). |

- **Linking verbs** (be, seem, look, feel, smell, taste, sound, appear, become, grow) take an **adjective**, not an adverb 🔥: "The rose **smells sweet**" (not *sweetly*). "She **looks sad**." "I **feel bad**." "The food **tastes good**."
- Same form as adjective and adverb: **fast, early, daily, straight, far, long, enough**. "**Fastly**" does not exist.

## Very / much / too / enough 🔥
- **very** + positive adjective/present participle: "**very** good", "**very** interesting".
- **much** + comparative/past participle: "**much better**", "**much** surprised", "**much** obliged".
- **too** = more than needed (negative sense): "The tea is **too hot to drink**." Don't use *too* for *very*: "He is **very** kind" (not *too kind* as praise).
- **too … to** = so … that … not: "He is **too weak to walk**" = "He is **so weak that he cannot walk**."
- **enough** comes **after** an adjective/adverb but **before** a noun: "He is **old enough** to vote." "We have **enough money**."
- **so … that**: "He is **so** tired **that** he can't work."

## Position of adverbs
- **Frequency adverbs** go **before the main verb** but **after "be"** and after the first auxiliary: "He **always** comes late." "He **is always** late." "I **have never** seen a tiger."
- **only** stands **next to the word it modifies** 🔥:
  - "**Only** Rahim passed." (no one else)
  - "Rahim **only** passed." / "Rahim passed **only** in English." — meaning changes with position.
- Order at the end of a sentence: **manner – place – time** (MPT): "He worked **hard at the office yesterday**."
- **Inversion after negative adverbs** at the start 🔥: **never, seldom, rarely, hardly, scarcely, not only, nowhere, little, at no time, on no account** → auxiliary before subject:
  - "**Never have I** seen such a sight."
  - "**Seldom does he** come here."
  - "**Little did he** know the danger."
  - "**Not only did he** help me, but he also lent me money."

## Other points
- **ago** is used with past simple; **before** with past perfect: "He left two years **ago**." "He **had** left two years **before**."
- **already** (affirmative) vs **yet** (negative/question): "I have **already** eaten." "Has he come **yet**?"
- **hardly/scarcely/barely** are negatives: don't add *not* ("I can **hardly** hear you", not *can't hardly*).
- **ever** after superlatives and in questions; **never** is negative.

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He sings very good. | He sings very **well**. |
| The flower smells sweetly. | The flower smells **sweet**. |
| I am very much happy. | I am **very** happy. |
| He is enough strong. | He is **strong enough**. |
| He can't hardly walk. | He can **hardly** walk. |
| Never I have seen him. | Never **have I** seen him. |
| He is very much taller than me. | He is **much** taller than I. |
| He comes always late. | He **always comes** late. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **hardly** = almost not; **lately** = recently; **nearly** = almost.
- 🔥 Linking verbs (**look, smell, taste, feel, seem**) + adjective.
- 🔥 **very** + positive; **much** + comparative/past participle.
- **enough** after an adjective, before a noun.
- **too … to** = so … that … not.
- Negative adverb first → **inversion**: "Never have I…".
- Frequency adverbs: before main verb, after "be".
