ENG-16.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who wrote the first English novel, which novel is epistolary (*Pamela*), who is the "Father of the English novel", Johnson's *Dictionary* (1755), and Goldsmith's works across genres.

## Rise of the novel
- The English novel rose in the 18th century with the growth of the **middle class**, literacy and printing.
- The "**big four**" of the 18th-century novel: **Richardson, Fielding, Smollett, Sterne**.
- **Defoe's *Robinson Crusoe* (1719)** is often called the first English novel; **Richardson's *Pamela* (1740)** is often called the **first modern English novel** / first psychological novel. Exams accept *Pamela* when "first English novel" is asked with Richardson among the options, but check the options for Defoe.

## Samuel Richardson (1689–1761) 🔥
- A printer by profession; master of the **epistolary novel** (a novel written as **letters**).

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded*** 🔥 | **1740** | A servant girl, **Pamela Andrews**, resists her master **Mr B.** and finally marries him |
| ***Clarissa*** | **1747–48** | Longest novel in English; tragic heroine **Clarissa Harlowe**, villain **Lovelace** |
| ***Sir Charles Grandison*** | 1753 | A perfect gentleman hero |

## Henry Fielding (1707–1754) 🔥
- **"Father of the English novel"** — the title most exam guides give (some books give it to Defoe or Richardson).
- Called his novels "**comic epic poems in prose**". Also a magistrate who founded the **Bow Street Runners**.

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***Shamela*** | 1741 | Parody of *Pamela* |
| ***Joseph Andrews*** | **1742** | Began as a parody of *Pamela* (Joseph is Pamela's brother); **Parson Adams** |
| ***Jonathan Wild*** | 1743 | Satire on a criminal |
| ***Tom Jones*** 🔥 | **1749** | *The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling*; **Tom**, **Sophia Western**, **Squire Allworthy**, **Blifil** |
| ***Amelia*** | 1751 | |

## Other novelists
| Writer | Work |
|---|---|
| **Tobias Smollett** | ***Roderick Random*** (1748), *Peregrine Pickle*, ***Humphry Clinker*** (1771) — picaresque novels |
| **Laurence Sterne** | ***Tristram Shandy*** (1759–67) — experimental; forerunner of the **stream of consciousness**; *A Sentimental Journey* |
| **Horace Walpole** | ***The Castle of Otranto*** (1764) — **first Gothic novel** |

## Dr. Samuel Johnson (1709–1784) 🔥
- Critic, lexicographer, essayist, poet; the central figure of the **Age of Johnson**. Known as "**Dr. Johnson**" and "the **Great Cham** of literature" (Smollett's phrase).
- His life was written by **James Boswell** — ***The Life of Samuel Johnson* (1791)**, the most famous biography in English.

| Work | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| ***A Dictionary of the English Language*** 🔥 | **1755** | Took about **9 years**; about **40,000+** words; first great English dictionary |
| ***Rasselas*** (*The Prince of Abyssinia*) | **1759** | Philosophical romance; written in a week to pay his mother's funeral costs |
| ***Lives of the Poets*** | **1779–81** | Critical biographies of 52 poets; coined "metaphysical poets" in *Life of Cowley* |
| ***The Vanity of Human Wishes*** | 1749 | Poem, imitation of Juvenal |
| ***London*** | 1738 | Poem |
| *The Rambler* / *The Idler* | 1750–52 / 1758–60 | Periodical essays |
| Edition of **Shakespeare** | 1765 | Famous *Preface to Shakespeare* |

- Famous sayings: "**Patriotism is the last refuge of a scoundrel.**" — "**When a man is tired of London, he is tired of life.**"
- He founded **The Literary Club** (1764) with Reynolds, Burke, Goldsmith and others.

## Oliver Goldsmith (c. 1728–1774) 🔥
- Irish; member of Johnson's circle. He wrote in **every major form**: novel, drama, poem, essay. Johnson's epitaph praised him as one who "left scarcely any style of writing untouched, and touched nothing that he did not adorn."

| Work | Year | Genre |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Vicar of Wakefield*** 🔥 | **1766** | **Novel**; **Dr. Charles Primrose**, a kindly vicar, and his family |
| ***She Stoops to Conquer*** 🔥 | **1773** | **Comedy**; **Marlow** mistakes the Hardcastles' house for an inn; **Kate Hardcastle**, **Tony Lumpkin** |
| *The Good-Natured Man* | 1768 | Comedy |
| ***The Deserted Village*** | **1770** | **Poem**: "**Ill fares the land, to hastening ills a prey, / Where wealth accumulates, and men decay**"; the village is **Sweet Auburn** |
| *The Traveller* | 1764 | Poem |
| ***The Citizen of the World*** | 1762 | Essays as letters of a Chinese visitor (Lien Chi Altangi) |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 ***Pamela* (1740)** — Richardson — **epistolary novel**.
- 🔥 **Fielding** = "**Father of the English novel**"; ***Tom Jones* (1749)**.
- ***Joseph Andrews*** began as a parody of *Pamela*.
- 🔥 **Johnson's *Dictionary* (1755)**; his biography by **Boswell (1791)**.
- ***Rasselas*** = Johnson; ***Tristram Shandy*** = Sterne.
- 🔥 Goldsmith: ***The Vicar of Wakefield*** (novel), ***She Stoops to Conquer*** (comedy), ***The Deserted Village*** (poem).
- ***The Castle of Otranto*** = first Gothic novel (Walpole).

ENG-17.notes:
> **Why it matters:** "Appropriate preposition" is asked in almost every job exam: *angry with/at, abide by, comply with, congratulate on, die of/from, differ from/with, superior to*. Learn the fixed pairs.

## Basic prepositions of time and place
| Use | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **at** | exact time, small point | at 5 pm, at night, at the gate |
| **on** | days and dates, surface | on Friday, on 16 December, on the table |
| **in** | months, years, seasons, parts of day, big places | in 1971, in July, in the morning, in Dhaka |
| **since** | point of time (perfect tense) | since 2010, since Monday |
| **for** | period | for two hours |
| **by** | not later than | by 5 o'clock |
| **within** | before the end of a period | within a week |
| **between** | two | between you and me |
| **among** | more than two | Divide the mangoes among the boys. |
| **beside** | by the side of | He sat beside me. |
| **besides** | in addition to | Besides English, he knows French. |
| **into** | movement inside | He jumped into the river. |
| **in** | position inside | He is swimming in the river. |

## Appropriate prepositions (most asked) 🔥
### Adjective / verb + preposition
| Phrase | Example |
|---|---|
| **abide by** | abide by the law |
| **absorbed in** | absorbed in thought |
| **accused of** / **charged with** | accused of theft; charged with murder |
| **accustomed to** | accustomed to hard work |
| **afraid of** | afraid of dogs |
| **agree with** (person) / **to** (proposal) / **on** (point) | I agree with you; he agreed to my proposal |
| **angry with** (person) / **at** (thing) | angry with him; angry at his rudeness |
| **anxious about** (worried) / **for** (eager) | anxious about his health; anxious for success |
| **aware of** | aware of the danger |
| **believe in** | believe in God |
| **blind to** (faults) / **of** (an eye) | blind to his faults; blind of one eye |
| **careful of / about** | careful of your health |
| **comply with** 🔥 | comply with the rules |
| **confident of** | confident of success |
| **congratulate on** 🔥 | congratulate him on his success |
| **consist of** | Water consists of hydrogen and oxygen. |
| **deal in** (trade) / **with** (handle) | He deals in rice; deal with a problem |
| **depend on** | depends on you |
| **deprived of** | deprived of his rights |
| **die of** (disease) / **from** (cause) / **by** (violence) / **for** (country) 🔥 | died of cholera; died from overwork; died by the sword; died for the country |
| **differ from** (thing) / **with** (person, opinion) | differ with you on this point |
| **disgusted with** | disgusted with his behaviour |
| **fond of** | fond of music |
| **good at** / **weak in** | good at mathematics; weak in English |
| **guilty of** | guilty of murder |
| **indifferent to** | indifferent to praise |
| **insist on** | insisted on going |
| **interested in** | interested in politics |
| **jealous of** | jealous of his success |
| **married to** | She is married to a doctor. |
| **named after** | named after his grandfather |
| **obedient to** | obedient to parents |
| **prefer … to** | prefer tea to coffee |
| **prevent from** | prevent him from going |
| **proud of** | proud of our heritage |
| **refrain from** | refrain from smoking |
| **rely on / upon** | rely on him |
| **senior / junior / superior / inferior / prior to** | senior to me |
| **suffer from** | suffering from fever |
| **sure of** | sure of success |
| **tired of** (bored) / **tired from** (effort) | tired of waiting; tired from the journey |
| **true to** | true to his word |
| **wait for** (person) / **on** (serve) | wait for me; waiters wait on guests |

### Noun + preposition
**access to, answer to, cure for, desire for, key to, reason for, respect for, solution to, sympathy for / with, lack of, need for, apology for**.
- "There is no **cure for** this disease." — "**Key to** the door." — "**Solution to** the problem."

## Rules to remember
- **Verb + no preposition** 🔥: **discuss** (not *discuss about*), **describe**, **enter** (a room), **reach** (a place), **order**, **resemble**, **attack**, **marry**, **request**, **investigate**, **emphasize**, **comprise**. "We discussed the matter." "She married a doctor." "He resembles his father."
- **Preposition + gerund**: "He is fond **of reading**."
- Do not put a preposition at the end if it is already used earlier: "the house in which he lives" = "the house which he lives **in**", not both.
- **On/at the time of** vs **in time** (early enough) vs **on time** (punctual).
- **By bus, by train, on foot, in a car**.

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He is angry on me. | He is angry **with** me. |
| We discussed about the matter. | We **discussed** the matter. |
| He died with cholera. | He died **of** cholera. |
| I congratulate you for your success. | I congratulate you **on** your success. |
| He is senior than me. | He is senior **to** me. |
| She is married with a doctor. | She is married **to** a doctor. |
| He entered into the room. | He **entered** the room. |
| He is good in English. | He is good **at** English. |
| Divide it between the three boys. | Divide it **among** the three boys. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **abide by, comply with, congratulate on, insist on, refrain from**.
- 🔥 **die of** a disease, **from** a cause, **for** a cause/country.
- **angry with** a person, **at** a thing.
- **agree with** a person, **to** a proposal.
- **between** two, **among** more than two.
- **discuss, enter, reach, resemble, marry** take no preposition.
- **Latin comparatives + to**.

ENG-18.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about *Lyrical Ballads* (1798), Wordsworth's definition of poetry, "Poet of Nature", *The Prelude*, the Lake Poets, *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* (albatross), "willing suspension of disbelief" and *Kubla Khan*.

## The Romantic Movement (1798–1832)
- Started with ***Lyrical Ballads* (1798)**, a joint collection by **Wordsworth and Coleridge** 🔥. The **Preface** (added in the **1800** edition, enlarged 1802) is the **manifesto of English Romanticism**.
- Features: **love of nature**, **imagination**, emotion, the **common man** and rustic life, the **supernatural**, individualism, return to the past, lyric poetry.
- Influences: the **French Revolution (1789)**, Rousseau ("Return to nature").
- **Pre-Romantics / forerunners:** Thomas Gray (*Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard*, 1751), William Collins, William Cowper, **Robert Burns**, **William Blake** (*Songs of Innocence and of Experience*).
- **First generation:** Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey (the **Lake Poets**). **Second generation:** Byron, Shelley, Keats.
- **Lake Poets** 🔥: **Wordsworth, Coleridge and Robert Southey** — they lived in the **Lake District** of north-west England.

## William Wordsworth (1770–1850) 🔥
- Born at **Cockermouth**, Cumberland (Lake District). **Poet Laureate from 1843** (after Southey) till his death.
- Epithets: **"Poet of Nature"** / "High priest of Nature", "Worshipper of Nature". Keats called his style the "**egotistical sublime**".
- Definition of poetry 🔥: "**Poetry is the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings: it takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.**" (Preface to *Lyrical Ballads*)
- He said poetry should use "**a selection of the language really used by men**".
- Sister: **Dorothy Wordsworth** (journals).

## Samuel Taylor Coleridge (1772–1834) 🔥
- Poet, critic and philosopher; friend of Wordsworth. Addicted to **opium**.

ENG-19.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams test correlative pairs (*either … or, neither … nor, not only … but also, no sooner … than, hardly … when, both … and, whether … or*), "lest … should", "though … yet", and "unless/until" misuse.

## What a conjunction does
A **conjunction** joins words, phrases or clauses: "Rahim **and** Karim", "slow **but** sure", "I stayed home **because** it rained."

## Kinds of conjunction
### 1. Coordinating conjunctions
Join two equal parts. Remember **FANBOYS**: **for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so**.

| Type | Conjunctions | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Cumulative** (adding) | and, as well as, both … and, not only … but also | "He is rich **as well as** generous." |
| **Adversative** (contrast) | but, yet, still, however, whereas, while | "He is poor **but** honest." |
| **Alternative** (choice) | or, either … or, neither … nor, otherwise, else | "Hurry up, **or** you will miss the bus." |
| **Illative** (result) | so, therefore, hence, for | "He was ill, **so** he did not come." |

### 2. Subordinating conjunctions
Join a dependent clause to a main clause.

| Meaning | Conjunctions | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Time | when, while, before, after, since, until, till, as soon as | "Wait **till** I come." |
| Reason | because, since, as | "**As** it was late, we left." |
| Condition | if, unless, provided that, in case | "**Unless** you work hard, you will fail." |
| Purpose | so that, in order that, **lest** | "Walk fast **lest** you **should** miss the train." |
| Result | so … that, such … that | "He is **so** weak **that** he cannot walk." |
| Concession | though, although, even if | "**Though** he is poor, (**yet**) he is honest." |
| Comparison | than, as … as | "He is taller **than** I." |

### 3. Correlative conjunctions (used in pairs) 🔥
| Pair | Example |
|---|---|
| **either … or** | "**Either** you **or** he must go." |
| **neither … nor** | "He is **neither** rich **nor** poor." |
| **both … and** | "**Both** Rahim **and** Karim were present." |
| **not only … but also** | "He is **not only** clever **but also** hardworking." |
| **whether … or** | "I don't know **whether** he will come **or** not." |
| **though / although … yet** | "**Though** he tried, **yet** he failed." |
| **so … that** | "The box is **so** heavy **that** I cannot lift it." |
| **such … that / such … as** | "He is **such** a fool **that** everyone laughs at him." "**Such** a man **as** he is rare." |
| **as … as / so … as** | "He is **as** tall **as** you." "He is not **so** tall **as** you." |
| **no sooner … than** 🔥 | "**No sooner** had he come **than** she left." |
| **hardly / scarcely … when / before** 🔥 | "**Hardly** had he come **when** she left." |
| **rather … than / would rather … than** | "I would **rather** die **than** beg." |
| **other … than** | "I have no **other** friend **than** you." |

## Rules exams love 🔥
1. **No sooner** takes **than** — never *when* or *then*.
2. **Hardly / scarcely / barely** take **when** or **before** — never *than*.
3. **Lest** is followed by **should** (not *not*): "Work hard **lest** you **should** fail" (not *lest you should not fail* — *lest* already means "so that … not").
4. **Unless** and **until** already contain "not" — don't add another *not*: "**Unless** you **read**, you will fail." "Wait **until** I **return**."
5. **Though** can pair with **yet**, never with *but*: "**Though** he is poor, **but** honest" is wrong.
6. **Both … and** — never *both … as well as*; "both" is not used with negatives.
7. **Parallel structure**: the words after each part of a correlative pair must be of the same kind: "He is **not only** a poet **but also** a painter" (not *not only is a poet but also a painter*).
8. **Neither … nor** (not *neither … or*); **either … or** (not *either … nor*).
9. **Because** gives the reason; don't combine with *so* in one sentence: "**Because** he was ill, he did not come" (not *because … so*).
10. **Since** (time) needs a present perfect main clause: "It **has been** two years **since** he left."
11. **Scarcely / seldom / not only** at the start → inversion: "**Not only did** he come, but he also stayed."
12. **Doubt**: "I doubt **whether/if** he will come" (positive). "I don't doubt **that** he will come" (negative).

## "Than" and "as" with pronouns
"He is older **than I** (am)." "She loves you **as much as I** (do)."

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| No sooner had he left when it rained. | No sooner had he left **than** it rained. |
| Hardly had he gone than I came. | Hardly had he gone **when** I came. |
| Though he is poor but he is honest. | Though he is poor, **(yet)** he is honest. |
| Unless you do not work, you will fail. | **Unless you work**, you will fail. |
| Neither Rahim or Karim came. | Neither Rahim **nor** Karim came. |
| Both he as well as his brother came. | Both he **and** his brother came. |
| Because he was ill, so he did not come. | Because he was ill, he did not come. |
| Walk fast lest you should not miss the bus. | Walk fast lest you **should miss** the bus. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **No sooner … than**; **Hardly/Scarcely … when**.
- 🔥 **lest … should**; **unless/until** without *not*.
- **Though … yet** (not *but*).
- **Neither … nor**, **either … or**, **both … and**.
- Correlatives need **parallel structure**.
- **FANBOYS** = coordinating conjunctions.
- **so … that / such … that** = result.

ENG-20.notes:
> **Why it matters:** The younger Romantics are asked through famous lines ("A thing of beauty is a joy for ever", "If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?"), epithets ("Poet of beauty", "revolutionary poet"), *Adonais*, *Don Juan* and their early deaths.

## Second-generation Romantics
All three died young and abroad: **Keats (25, Rome, 1821)**, **Shelley (29, drowned in Italy, 1822)**, **Byron (36, Missolonghi, Greece, 1824)**.

## Lord Byron (George Gordon, 1788–1824) 🔥
- Aristocrat, rebel, satirist; the **"Byronic hero"** — proud, moody, mysterious, defiant outsider.
- After *Childe Harold* I–II (1812) he said: "**I awoke one morning and found myself famous.**"
- Died at **Missolonghi** while helping the **Greek War of Independence**; a national hero in Greece.

| Work | Year | Fact / famous line |
|---|---|---|
| ***Hours of Idleness*** | 1807 | First collection; savagely reviewed |
| ***English Bards and Scotch Reviewers*** | 1809 | Satire replying to the critics |
| ***Childe Harold's Pilgrimage*** | **1812–18** | In the **Spenserian stanza**; made him famous |
| ***Don Juan*** 🔥 | **1819–24** (unfinished) | Comic-satiric **epic** in **ottava rima**; includes "**The Isles of Greece**"; "**'Tis strange — but true; for truth is always strange; / Stranger than fiction**" |
| ***Manfred*** | 1817 | Dramatic poem |
| ***The Prisoner of Chillon*** | 1816 | |
| ***The Vision of Judgment*** | 1822 | Satire on **Southey** |
| "**She Walks in Beauty**" | 1815 | "She walks in beauty, like the night" |

## Percy Bysshe Shelley (1792–1822) 🔥
- Expelled from **Oxford** for ***The Necessity of Atheism* (1811)**.
- Epithets: **"Revolutionary poet"** / poet of revolt and idealism; **Matthew Arnold** called him "**a beautiful and ineffectual angel, beating in the void his luminous wings in vain**".
- Wife: **Mary Shelley**, author of ***Frankenstein* (1818)**.
- **Drowned** in the Gulf of **La Spezia**, Italy, in **1822**; his body was cremated on the beach.

| "**Ode to the West Wind**" 🔥 | **1819** (pub. 1820) | "**O wild West Wind**"; "**I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!**"; last line "**If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?**" |
| "**To a Skylark**" 🔥 | 1820 | "**Hail to thee, blithe Spirit!**"; "**Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought**" |
| "**The Cloud**" | 1820 | "I am the daughter of Earth and Water" |
| ***Prometheus Unbound*** 🔥 | **1820** | **Lyrical drama** in four acts |
| ***The Cenci*** | 1819 | Tragedy |

| ***A Defence of Poetry*** | 1821 (pub. 1840) | 🔥 "**Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world.**" |

## John Keats (1795–1821) 🔥
- Son of a stable-keeper in London; trained as an **apothecary/surgeon**.
- Epithets: **"Poet of beauty"**, "worshipper of beauty", "poet of the senses" (sensuousness).
- His critical ideas are in his **letters**: "**Negative Capability**" (1817) — the ability to live with "uncertainties, mysteries, doubts" — and the "**egotistical sublime**" (about Wordsworth).
- Died of **tuberculosis** in **Rome** in 1821, aged **25**. His epitaph: "**Here lies one whose name was writ in water.**"

|---|---|---|
| "**On First Looking into Chapman's Homer**" | 1816 | Sonnet; "Much have I travelled in the realms of gold" |

| ***Lamia***, ***Isabella*** | 1820 | Narrative poems |

### The Great Odes (1819) 🔥
| Ode | Famous line |
|---|---|
| "**Ode to a Nightingale**" | "**My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains / My sense**"; "**Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!**" |
| "**Ode on a Grecian Urn**" | "**Beauty is truth, truth beauty, — that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know**"; "**Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter**"; "Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness" |
| "**To Autumn**" | "**Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness**" |
| "**Ode on Melancholy**" | |
| "**Ode to Psyche**" | |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 "**A thing of beauty is a joy for ever**" — Keats, *Endymion*.
- 🔥 "**Beauty is truth, truth beauty**" — Keats, *Ode on a Grecian Urn*.
- 🔥 "**If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?**" — Shelley, *Ode to the West Wind*.
- ***Adonais*** — Shelley's elegy on **Keats**.
- "**Poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world**" — Shelley.
- 🔥 ***Don Juan*** — Byron, **ottava rima**; Byron died at **Missolonghi**.
- Keats = "**Poet of beauty**"; "**Negative Capability**".
- "Beautiful and ineffectual angel" — **Arnold** on Shelley.

ENG-21.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Article questions test sound-based "a/an" (an hour, a university, an MA, a one-taka note), "the" with rivers, seas, unique things and superlatives, and when no article is used (go to school, by bus).

## The articles
- **Indefinite:** **a, an** — one, any, not particular.
- **Definite:** **the** — a particular, known thing.
- Articles are a kind of **adjective** (demonstrative adjective / determiner).

## A or An? — it depends on SOUND, not spelling 🔥
| Use **an** before a vowel **sound** | Use **a** before a consonant **sound** |
|---|---|
| **an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour** (silent h) | **a university, a union, a European, a useful book, a uniform** ("yu" sound) |
| **an MA, an MBBS doctor, an SSC certificate, an LLB, an FIR, an X-ray, an NGO, an MP, an SI** (letter name starts with a vowel sound: "em", "es", "el", "ef", "ex", "en") | **a one-taka note, a one-eyed man, a once-famous actor** ("w" sound) |
| an apple, an egg, an umbrella, an ugly face | **a BA, a BSc, a UN officer, a hotel, a historical event** (usually), a horse |
| **an F grade** | **a U-turn** |

Tip: say the word aloud. "**An** hour" (sounds "our"), "**a** university" (sounds "yu").

## Uses of "a / an"
- One: "He has **a** car."
- Profession: "He is **a** doctor."
- Rate: "Tk 50 **a** kilo", "twice **a** day", "60 km **an** hour".
- Exclamation: "What **a** beautiful day!" "Such **a** fool!"
- Before a proper noun used as a common noun: "He is **a** Shakespeare of our age." "**A** Mr Karim came to see you."
- Fixed phrases: **a few, a little, a lot of, a great deal of, a number of, in a hurry, at a loss, all of a sudden, make a noise, take a walk, have a headache**.

## Uses of "the" 🔥
| Rule | Examples |
|---|---|
| Something already mentioned or known | "I saw a dog. **The** dog was black." |
| **Unique things** | **the sun, the moon, the earth, the sky, the world** |
| **Rivers, seas, oceans, canals, gulfs** | **the Padma, the Jamuna, the Bay of Bengal, the Pacific, the Suez Canal** |
| **Mountain ranges, groups of islands, deserts** | **the Himalayas, the Andes, the Maldives, the Sahara** |
| **Holy books, newspapers, ships, trains** | **the Quran, the Bible, the Daily Star, the Titanic** |
| Countries with plural or "union/kingdom/states/republic" | **the USA, the UK, the Netherlands, the Philippines, the People's Republic of China** |
| **Superlatives and ordinals** | **the best, the tallest, the first, the last** |
| **the + adjective** = a class of people | **the rich, the poor, the brave, the young** |
| **the + singular noun** = the whole class | "**The** cow is a useful animal." "**The** rose is sweet." |
| Musical instruments | "She plays **the** piano / **the** guitar." |
| Nationality (people) | **the English, the Bangalees, the Japanese** |
| Directions, historical events | **the east, the north; the French Revolution, the Liberation War** |
| **the + comparative, the + comparative** | "**The** more, **the** merrier." |
| Proper noun with a qualifying phrase | "**the** Dhaka of today", "**the** Bangladesh of 1971" |
| Name of a great work as a comparison | "Kalidasa is called **the** Shakespeare of India." |

## No article 🔥
- **Proper names** of persons, cities, countries, single mountains, lakes: **Dhaka, Bangladesh, Mount Everest, Lake Victoria** (but *the Himalayas*).
- **Uncountable and abstract nouns** in a general sense: "**Honesty** is the best policy." "**Gold** is precious." "**Milk** is good for health."
- **Meals, games, languages, subjects:** "have **breakfast**", "play **cricket**", "speak **English**", "study **mathematics**".
- **School, college, church, mosque, hospital, prison, bed, market** used for their **main purpose**: "He goes **to school**" (to study). "He is **in hospital**" (as a patient). But "He went **to the school** to meet the teacher" (visit the building).
- **Transport with "by":** **by bus, by train, by air**; also **at night, at home, at noon, on foot**.
- Days, months, seasons (usually), and **man** meaning mankind: "**Man** is mortal."
- Titles used as names: "**Queen** Elizabeth", "**President** Lincoln"; but "**the** President of Bangladesh".

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He is a honest man. | He is **an** honest man. |
| She is an university student. | She is **a** university student. |
| He has a MA degree. | He has **an** MA degree. |
| Padma is a big river. | **The** Padma is a big river. |
| The honesty is the best policy. | **Honesty** is the best policy. |
| He goes to the bed at 10. | He goes **to bed** at 10. |
| She plays piano. (exam style) | She plays **the** piano. |
| He is best boy in the class. | He is **the** best boy in the class. |
| I came here by the bus. | I came here **by bus**. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 a/an depends on **sound**: **an hour, an MA, a university, a one-taka note**.
- 🔥 **the** + rivers, seas, mountain ranges, unique things, superlatives.
- **the + adjective** = a class of people (the rich).
- **No article** with proper names, abstract/material nouns in general, meals, games, languages.
- **go to school / bed / hospital** (purpose) — no article.
- **by bus, by train, at night, on foot**.
- **the USA, the UK, the Himalayas**, but **Mount Everest**.

ENG-22.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about *In Memoriam* (for Arthur Hallam), "Ulysses", Tennyson as Poet Laureate, Browning's dramatic monologue ("My Last Duchess"), Arnold's "Dover Beach" and his definition of poetry as "criticism of life".

## The Victorian Age (1832–1901)
- Named after **Queen Victoria** (reigned **1837–1901**).
- Themes: industrial progress and its costs, **conflict of science and faith** (Darwin's ***On the Origin of Species*, 1859**), doubt, moral earnestness, social reform.
- Other poets: **Elizabeth Barrett Browning** (*Sonnets from the Portuguese*: "**How do I love thee? Let me count the ways**"), **D. G. Rossetti** and the **Pre-Raphaelites**, **Christina Rossetti** (*Goblin Market*), **Swinburne**, **Gerard Manley Hopkins** ("sprung rhythm", published 1918), **Edward FitzGerald** (translated ***The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam***, 1859).
- Prose thinkers: **Thomas Carlyle** (*Sartor Resartus*, *Heroes and Hero-Worship*), **John Ruskin** (*Unto This Last*, *Modern Painters*), **J. S. Mill** (*On Liberty*).

## Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1809–1892) 🔥
- **Poet Laureate from 1850 to 1892** (after Wordsworth) — the longest-serving; made a **Baron (Lord)** in 1884.
- Epithet: the **representative poet of the Victorian age**.

ENG-23.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Voice-change questions give an active sentence and ask for the correct passive (or the reverse). Tricky types: questions, imperatives, "let", two objects, "known to", "It is said that", and verbs with prepositions.

## Basics
- **Active voice:** the subject **does** the action — "Rahim **wrote** a letter."
- **Passive voice:** the subject **receives** the action — "A letter **was written** by Rahim."
- Formula: **Object → subject + be (in the right tense) + past participle (V3) + by + agent**.
- Only **transitive verbs** (with an object) can be changed into the passive. "He sleeps" has no passive.

## Pronoun changes
| Active | I | we | you | he | she | they | it | who |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Passive (by …)** | me | us | you | him | her | them | it | **whom** |

## Tense table 🔥
| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Present simple | He **writes** a letter. | A letter **is written** by him. |
| Present continuous | He **is writing** a letter. | A letter **is being written** by him. |
| Present perfect | He **has written** a letter. | A letter **has been written** by him. |
| Past simple | He **wrote** a letter. | A letter **was written** by him. |
| Past continuous | He **was writing** a letter. | A letter **was being written** by him. |
| Past perfect | He **had written** a letter. | A letter **had been written** by him. |
| Future simple | He **will write** a letter. | A letter **will be written** by him. |
| Future perfect | He **will have written** a letter. | A letter **will have been written** by him. |
| Modal | He **can / must / should write** a letter. | A letter **can / must / should be written** by him. |
| going to | He **is going to write** a letter. | A letter **is going to be written** by him. |

- **Perfect continuous tenses and the future continuous** are normally **not changed** into the passive.

## Special cases 🔥
### 1. Interrogative sentences
| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| **Did** he **write** the letter? | **Was** the letter **written** by him? |
| **Do** you **know** him? | **Is** he **known to** you? |
| **Who** wrote this? | **By whom was** this **written**? |
| **What** are you doing? | **What is being done** by you? |
| **Why** did he beat the dog? | **Why was** the dog **beaten** by him? |

### 2. Imperative sentences — use **Let**
| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| **Shut** the door. | **Let the door be shut.** |
| **Do not** insult the poor. | **Let not** the poor **be insulted**. / Let the poor not be insulted. |
| **Help** me. | **Let me be helped.** |
| **Please help** me. / Kindly lend me your pen. | **You are requested to** help me. |
| **Obey** your parents. (advice) | **You are advised to** obey your parents. |
| **Leave** the room. (order) | **You are ordered to** leave the room. |
| **Let** him do the work. | **Let the work be done by him.** |

### 3. Two objects
"The teacher **gave me** a book." →
- "**I was given** a book by the teacher." (personal object as subject — preferred)
- "**A book was given (to) me** by the teacher."

### 4. Verbs that don't take "by" 🔥
| Verb | Preposition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **know** | **to** | "He is **known to** me." (not *by me*) |
| **please / satisfy / disappoint** | **with** | "I am **pleased with** your work." |
| **surprise / astonish** | **at** | "I was **surprised at** his behaviour." |
| **interest** | **in** | "He is **interested in** music." |
| **fill** | **with** | "The glass **is filled with** water." |
| **cover** | **with** | "The field is **covered with** snow." |
| **marry** | **to** | "She **was married to** a doctor." |
| **contain** | **in** | "Sugar **is contained in** the box." |
| **vex / annoy** | **with / at** | "I am **annoyed with** him." |

### 5. Verb + preposition (phrasal)
Keep the preposition: "They **laughed at** the beggar." → "The beggar **was laughed at** by them." "We must **look after** the old." → "The old **must be looked after**."

### 6. "It is said / believed / known that"
"People **say** that he is honest." →
- "**It is said that** he is honest." or
- "He **is said to be** honest."
"People believe that he was a spy." → "He **is believed to have been** a spy."

### 7. Omit "by + agent" when it is unimportant or unknown
"Someone **has stolen** my pen." → "My pen **has been stolen**." "They **speak English** all over the world." → "English **is spoken** all over the world."

### 8. Passive → active (reverse)
"The work **is being done** by them." → "They **are doing** the work." "By whom was the glass broken?" → "**Who broke** the glass?"

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He is known by me. | He is known **to** me. |
| Let the door is shut. | Let the door **be** shut. |
| By who was it done? | By **whom** was it done? |
| The beggar was laughed by them. | The beggar was laughed **at** by them. |
| A letter is wrote by him. | A letter is **written** by him. |
| I am pleased by your work. | I am pleased **with** your work. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Passive = **be + V3**; continuous = **being + V3**; perfect = **been + V3**.
- 🔥 Imperative → **Let + object + be + V3**; requests → "**You are requested to**".
- 🔥 **known to, pleased with, surprised at, interested in, filled with, married to**.
- **Who → By whom**.
- Prepositions of phrasal verbs remain (**laughed at**, **looked after**).
- Intransitive verbs have **no passive**.
- "People say …" → "**It is said that …**" / "He **is said to be** …".

ENG-24.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask for the author of a novel or character (Oliver Twist, Pip, Heathcliff, Tess, Maggie Tulliver), pen names (Boz, Currer/Ellis/Acton Bell, George Eliot), Hardy's Wessex, and famous first lines.

## The Victorian novel
- The **novel** was the dominant form of the Victorian age; many were **serialised** in magazines.
- Themes: poverty, industrial cities, class, education, women's position, faith and doubt.
- Other novelists: **W. M. Thackeray** — ***Vanity Fair*** (1847–48), heroine **Becky Sharp**, subtitle "A Novel without a Hero"; **Anthony Trollope** — *Barsetshire* novels; **Elizabeth Gaskell** — *Mary Barton*, *Cranford*, *North and South*; **Wilkie Collins** — ***The Moonstone*** (1868), often called the first full-length English detective novel; **Lewis Carroll** — ***Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*** (1865); **R. L. Stevenson** — *Treasure Island*, *Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* (1886).

## Charles Dickens (1812–1870) 🔥
- The most popular Victorian novelist; pen name **"Boz"** (*Sketches by Boz*, 1836). Worked in a **blacking factory** as a child when his father was in a debtors' prison.
- Famous for **social criticism**, humour, memorable **caricatures**, orphan heroes.

Daughters of a clergyman at **Haworth**, Yorkshire. They first published under male pen names.

## George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans, 1819–1880) 🔥
- **"George Eliot" is the pen name of Mary Ann (Marian) Evans** — a woman using a male name. Partner: **G. H. Lewes**.
- Known for **psychological realism** and moral seriousness; many novels are set in the English **Midlands**.

## Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) 🔥
- Novelist and poet; trained as an **architect**. Set his novels in **"Wessex"**, a fictional version of **south-west England (Dorset)**.

ENG-25.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Narration questions ask for the correct indirect form of a statement, question, command or exclamation — testing the reporting verb (asked, ordered, exclaimed), tense back-shift, pronoun change, and time/place words (now → then).

## Direct and indirect speech
- **Direct:** the speaker's exact words inside inverted commas — He said, "**I am ill.**"
- **Indirect:** the words reported in our own words — He said that **he was ill**.
- Parts: **reporting verb** (said) + **reported speech** (the words spoken).

## Rule 1: Tense change 🔥
If the reporting verb is in the **past**, the tense of the reported speech goes **one step back**:

| Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|
| present simple (**am/is/write**) | past simple (**was/wrote**) |
| present continuous (**is writing**) | past continuous (**was writing**) |
| present perfect (**has written**) | past perfect (**had written**) |
| past simple (**wrote**) | past perfect (**had written**) |
| past continuous (**was writing**) | past perfect continuous (**had been writing**) |
| **will / shall** | **would / should** |
| **can / may** | **could / might** |
| **must** | **had to** (or **must** unchanged) |

**No tense change when** 🔥:
- The reporting verb is **present or future**: He **says**, "I am ill." → He says that he **is** ill.
- The reported speech is a **universal truth / habitual fact**: The teacher said, "The earth **moves** round the sun." → The teacher said that the earth **moves** round the sun.
- Past perfect, and **could, would, should, might, ought to** stay the same.

## Rule 2: Pronoun change (SON rule)
- **1st person** (I, we, my) → changes to the person of the **Subject** of the reporting verb.
- **2nd person** (you, your) → changes to the person of the **Object** of the reporting verb.
- **3rd person** → **No** change.
- Example: He said to me, "**You** are late." → He told me that **I** was late.

## Rule 3: Words of time and place 🔥
| Direct | Indirect | Direct | Indirect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **now** | **then** | **today** | **that day** |
| **here** | **there** | **tonight** | **that night** |
| **this** | **that** | **tomorrow** | **the next day / the following day** |
| **these** | **those** | **yesterday** | **the previous day / the day before** |
| **ago** | **before** | **last night** | **the previous night** |
| **thus** | **so** | **next week** | **the following week** |
| **come** | **go** (when place changes) | **hence** | **thence** |

## Rule 4: By type of sentence
### Assertive (statement)
**said → said**, **said to → told**; connector **that**.
- He said to me, "I will help you." → He **told** me **that** he **would** help me.

### Interrogative (question) 🔥
Reporting verb → **asked / enquired / wanted to know**; question becomes a **statement form** (no question mark); no "that".
- **Yes/No question** → **if / whether**: He said to me, "**Are** you ill?" → He asked me **if I was** ill.
- **Wh-question** → the **wh-word** is kept: She said to him, "**Where do** you live?" → She asked him **where he lived**.
- Don't write "He asked me where **did I live**".

### Imperative (command, request, advice)
Reporting verb → **ordered / commanded / told** (command), **requested** (please, kindly), **advised** (advice), **forbade** (don't); verb → **to + V1**.
- He said to me, "**Go** home." → He **ordered me to go** home.
- She said to him, "**Please** help me." → She **requested him to help** her.
- The teacher said, "**Don't** make a noise." → The teacher **forbade** us **to make** a noise. / … told us **not to make** a noise.
- **Let's** (proposal) → **proposed / suggested that … should**: He said, "**Let us** go out." → He **proposed that they should** go out.

### Optative (wish, prayer)
**wished / prayed** + that + **might**:
- She said to me, "**May** you be happy!" → She **wished that I might** be happy. — "**May Allah bless you**" → He **prayed that** Allah **might bless** me.

### Exclamatory
**exclaimed with joy / sorrow / surprise / wonder**; turn into a statement:
- He said, "**Hurrah!** We have won." → He **exclaimed with joy that** they had won.
- She said, "**Alas!** I am ruined." → She **exclaimed with sorrow that** she was ruined.
- He said, "**What a** fine day it is!" → He **exclaimed that** it was **a very fine** day.

### Special words
- "**Yes**"/"**No**" → **replied in the affirmative / negative**.
- "**Good morning**" → **wished** (someone) **good morning**; "**Thank you**" → **thanked**; "**Sir**" → **respectfully**.

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| He said me that he was ill. | He **told** me that he was ill. |
| He asked me that where I lived. | He asked me **where I lived**. |
| He asked me where did I live. | He asked me where **I lived**. |
| She told me that she will come tomorrow. | She told me that she **would** come **the next day**. |
| He ordered me that go. | He ordered me **to go**. |
| The teacher said the sun rose in the east. | … the sun **rises** in the east. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 Past reporting verb → **one tense back**; **will → would, can → could**.
- 🔥 **Universal truth** → no tense change.
- 🔥 **now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day, ago → before**.
- Question → **asked + if/whether** or **wh-word**, statement word order.
- Command → **ordered/requested/advised + to + V1**; "Don't" → **forbade / told … not to**.
- **Let's** → **proposed/suggested that … should**.
- Exclamation → **exclaimed with joy/sorrow**.

> **Why it matters:** Exams ask about *The Waste Land* (1922), Eliot's Nobel Prize (1948), "April is the cruellest month", "objective correlative", Yeats's Nobel (1923), "The Second Coming", "Sailing to Byzantium" and the Irish Literary Revival.

## Modernism (c. 1901–1939)
- A break with Victorian tradition after the shock of **World War I**: fragmentation, alienation, loss of faith, **free verse**, allusion, myth, **stream of consciousness** in fiction.
- **Imagism** (c. 1912–17): clear, precise images — **Ezra Pound** ("In a Station of the Metro"), H. D., Amy Lowell. Pound's motto: "**Make it new.**"
- **War poets:** **Wilfred Owen** ("Dulce et Decorum Est", "Anthem for Doomed Youth"; "**My subject is War, and the pity of War**"), **Siegfried Sassoon**, **Rupert Brooke** ("The Soldier": "some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England").
- **Georgian poets:** Walter de la Mare, John Masefield ("Sea-Fever"), W. H. Davies ("Leisure": "What is this life if, full of care, / We have no time to stand and stare").

## W. B. Yeats (1865–1939) 🔥
- **Irish** poet and dramatist; won the **Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923** 🔥 — the first Irish writer to win it.
- Leader of the **Irish Literary Revival (Celtic Revival)**; co-founded the **Abbey Theatre, Dublin (1904)** with **Lady Gregory**.
- Became a **Senator** of the Irish Free State (1922).
- Loved the Irish revolutionary **Maud Gonne**, who refused his proposals.
- Interested in mysticism and the occult; his system is in ***A Vision*** (1925): history moves in **gyres** (cycles of about 2,000 years).
- Widely regarded as one of the **greatest 20th-century poets in English**; his style moved from dreamy Celtic romanticism to hard, modern symbolism.

| Work | Year | Fact / famous line |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Wanderings of Oisin*** | 1889 | Early long poem on Irish legend |
| "**The Lake Isle of Innisfree**" 🔥 | **1890** | "**I will arise and go now, and go to Innisfree**" |
| "**When You Are Old**" | 1892 | Addressed to Maud Gonne |
| ***The Wind Among the Reeds*** | 1899 | |
| ***Cathleen ni Houlihan*** | 1902 | Nationalist play (with Lady Gregory) |
| "**Easter, 1916**" 🔥 | 1916 (pub. 1920) | On the Dublin Easter Rising: "**A terrible beauty is born.**" |
| ***The Wild Swans at Coole*** | 1917/1919 | "The Wild Swans at Coole"; "An Irish Airman Foresees His Death" |
| "**The Second Coming**" 🔥 | **1919** (pub. 1920) | "**Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold; / Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world**"; "**The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity**"; "rough beast … Slouches towards Bethlehem" |
| "**A Prayer for My Daughter**" | 1919 | |
| ***The Tower*** | **1928** | Includes "**Sailing to Byzantium**" 🔥 ("**That is no country for old men**") and "**Leda and the Swan**" |
| ***The Winding Stair*** | 1933 | "Byzantium" |
| "**Among School Children**" | 1928 | "**How can we know the dancer from the dance?**" |

- Chinua Achebe took the title ***Things Fall Apart*** (1958) from "The Second Coming".

## T. S. Eliot (1888–1965) 🔥
- Born in **St Louis, USA**; settled in England and became a **British citizen in 1927** (same year he joined the Church of England).
- Won the **Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948** 🔥 and the **Order of Merit**.
- Worked at Lloyds Bank, then as an editor at **Faber and Faber**; edited the journal *The Criterion*.
- The most influential **poet-critic of modernism**; his essays shaped the later "New Criticism".

| Work | Year | Fact / famous line |
|---|---|---|
| "**The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock**" 🔥 | **1915** (in *Prufrock and Other Observations*, 1917) | "**Let us go then, you and I, / When the evening is spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherised upon a table**"; "**I have measured out my life with coffee spoons**"; "I grow old … I grow old" |
| "**Preludes**", "**Gerontion**" | 1917 / 1920 | |
| ***The Waste Land*** 🔥🔥 | **1922** | Dedicated to **Ezra Pound** ("*il miglior fabbro*" — "the better craftsman"), who edited it; **five sections**: "The Burial of the Dead", "A Game of Chess", "The Fire Sermon", "Death by Water", "What the Thunder Said". Opening: "**April is the cruellest month**". Ends with "**Shantih shantih shantih**" (from the Upanishads). Speaker figure: **Tiresias** |
| "**The Hollow Men**" | **1925** | "**This is the way the world ends / Not with a bang but a whimper.**" |
| "**Journey of the Magi**" | 1927 | After his conversion |
| ***Ash-Wednesday*** | 1930 | Religious poem |
| ***Murder in the Cathedral*** 🔥 | **1935** | **Verse drama** on the murder of **Archbishop Thomas Becket** at Canterbury (1170) |
| ***Four Quartets*** | **1943** (as a book) | "Burnt Norton", "East Coker", "The Dry Salvages", "Little Gidding": "In my beginning is my end" |
| ***The Family Reunion***, ***The Cocktail Party*** | 1939, 1949 | Verse plays |
| ***Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats*** | 1939 | Basis of the musical *Cats* |

### Eliot's criticism 🔥
| Essay / book | Key idea |
|---|---|
| "**Tradition and the Individual Talent**" (**1919**) | "**Impersonal theory of poetry**": "Poetry is not a turning loose of emotion, but an **escape from emotion**"; the poet as a **catalyst** (platinum) |
| "**Hamlet and His Problems**" (1919) | "**Objective correlative**"; he called *Hamlet* "most certainly an artistic failure" |
| "**The Metaphysical Poets**" (1921) | "**Dissociation of sensibility**" after the 17th century |
| ***The Sacred Wood*** (1920) | His first collection of essays |

- Eliot described himself as "**classicist in literature, royalist in politics, and Anglo-Catholic in religion**".

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **Yeats** — Irish, **Nobel 1923**, Abbey Theatre, "**Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold**" (*The Second Coming*).
- "**A terrible beauty is born**" — *Easter, 1916*; "**That is no country for old men**" — *Sailing to Byzantium*.
- 🔥 **Eliot** — ***The Waste Land* (1922)**, **Nobel 1948**, "**April is the cruellest month**".
- *The Waste Land* dedicated to **Ezra Pound**; ends "**Shantih shantih shantih**".
- "**Not with a bang but a whimper**" — *The Hollow Men*.
- ***Murder in the Cathedral*** — Becket; **objective correlative** — Eliot.
- **Prufrock**: "measured out my life with coffee spoons".

ENG-27.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask you to change a sentence without changing its meaning: simple ↔ complex ↔ compound, affirmative ↔ negative, degree of comparison, assertive ↔ interrogative/exclamatory, and "too … to" ↔ "so … that".

## Kinds of sentence by structure 🔥
| Kind | Structure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple** | **one** finite verb (one main clause) | "**Being ill**, he could not come." |
| **Compound** | **two or more main clauses** joined by coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so, therefore) | "He was ill, **and so** he could not come." |
| **Complex** | **one main clause + one or more subordinate clauses** (because, if, when, who, that, though) | "**As he was ill**, he could not come." |

## Simple ↔ Complex ↔ Compound 🔥
| Simple | Complex | Compound |
|---|---|---|
| **Being** poor, he could not buy it. | **As** he was poor, he could not buy it. | He was poor **and so** he could not buy it. |
| **In spite of** being rich, he is unhappy. | **Though** he is rich, he is unhappy. | He is rich, **but** he is unhappy. |
| **Without** working hard, you cannot succeed. | **If** you **do not** work hard / **Unless** you work hard, you cannot succeed. | Work hard, **or** you cannot succeed. |
| He confessed **his guilt**. | He confessed **that he was guilty**. | He was guilty **and** he confessed it. |
| **At sunrise** we started. | We started **when** the sun rose. | The sun rose **and** we started. |
| He is too weak **to walk**. | He is **so** weak **that** he cannot walk. | He is very weak **and so** he cannot walk. |
| I saw a **wounded** bird. | I saw a bird **which was wounded**. | I saw a bird **and** it was wounded. |
| He worked hard **to pass**. | He worked hard **so that he might pass**. | He wanted to pass, **so** he worked hard. |

### Key conversion tools
| Simple uses | Complex uses | Compound uses |
|---|---|---|
| participle (**being, having + V3**) | **as, since, because** | **and, so, therefore** |
| **in spite of / despite** + noun/gerund | **though / although** | **but, yet, still** |
| **without** + gerund; **by** + gerund | **if / unless** | **or, otherwise, else** |
| **to** + infinitive (purpose) | **so that / in order that** | **and** |
| **too … to** | **so … that … not** | **very … and so … not** |
| noun / phrase | noun / adjective / adverb clause | two main clauses |

## Affirmative ↔ Negative 🔥
| Affirmative | Negative |
|---|---|
| He is **always** punctual. | He is **never** late / **never** unpunctual. |
| **Only** Rahim can do it. | **None but** Rahim can do it. |
| **Only** a fool can say this. | **None but** a fool can say this. |
| He is **only** ten. | He is **not more than** ten. |
| **Everyone** loves his country. | **There is no one who does not** love his country. |
| As soon as he came, I left. | **No sooner** had he come **than** I left. |
| I **doubt** whether he will come. | I **am not sure** that he will come. |
| He is **greater** than I. | I am **not so great as** he. |
| I **remember** the day. | I **do not forget** the day. |
| He **failed** to come. | He **did not come**. |
| He is **honest**. | He is **not dishonest**. |
| Both of them came. | **Not only** X **but also** Y came. |

## Degrees of comparison 🔥
| Superlative | Comparative | Positive |
|---|---|---|
| Rahim is **the tallest** boy in the class. | Rahim is **taller than any other** boy in the class. | **No other** boy in the class is **as tall as** Rahim. |
| Dhaka is **one of the largest** cities in Asia. | Dhaka is **larger than most other** cities in Asia. | **Very few** cities in Asia are **as large as** Dhaka. |
| Shakespeare is **the greatest** dramatist. | Shakespeare is **greater than any other** dramatist. | **No other** dramatist is **as great as** Shakespeare. |

- "**one of the + superlative**" → "**than most other**" → "**very few … as … as**".
- Comparative "A is better than B" → Positive "**B is not so good as A**".

## Assertive ↔ Interrogative ↔ Exclamatory
| Assertive | Interrogative / Exclamatory |
|---|---|
| **Everybody** knows him. | **Who** does not know him? |
| **Nobody** can do it. | **Who** can do it? |
| It is **no use** crying. | **What is the use of** crying? |
| He **never** tells a lie. | **Does** he **ever** tell a lie? |
| It is a **very** fine day. | **What a** fine day it is! |
| He is **very** clever. | **How** clever he is! |
| I **wish** I were young again. | **Would that** I were young again! / **If only** I were young again! |

Note: an **affirmative** assertive becomes a **negative** rhetorical question, and vice versa.

## Imperative ↔ Assertive
- "**Do** it." → "You **should** do it." — "**Don't** smoke." → "You **should not** smoke." — "**Let** us go." → "**We should** go."

## Active ↔ Passive / Direct ↔ Indirect
These are also "transformation", covered in the voice-change and narration notes.

## Common mistakes
| Wrong | Right |
|---|---|
| Inspite of he is rich, he is unhappy. | **In spite of being** rich, he is unhappy. / **Though** he is rich, … |
| He is too weak that he cannot walk. | He is **so** weak **that** he cannot walk. |
| No other boy is taller than Rahim. (as the positive form) | No other boy is **as tall as** Rahim. |
| Rahim is taller than any boy in the class. | … **than any other** boy … |
| Though he is poor but he is honest. | **Though** he is poor, he is honest. / He is poor **but** honest. |

## Quick revision
- 🔥 **Simple** = one finite verb; **compound** = two main clauses; **complex** = main + subordinate.
- 🔥 **too … to** ↔ **so … that … not**.
- 🔥 **in spite of** (simple) ↔ **though** (complex) ↔ **but** (compound).
- **Only** → **none but** (person), **not more than** (number).
- Superlative → **than any other** → **no other … as … as**.
- **Everybody knows** → "**Who does not know**?"
- **very** → "**What a / How**" (exclamatory).

ENG-28.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask "Who wrote X?", "X is a character of which novel?", and the technique a writer is known for, such as stream of consciousness or political allegory. The modern period is roughly **1900–1945**.

## Features of the modern period
- Break with Victorian certainty after **World War I**; loss of faith, alienation, fragmentation.
- 🔥 **Stream of consciousness**: showing the flow of a character's thoughts. The term was first used by psychologist **William James**. Main novelists: **James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, Dorothy Richardson**.
- **Interior monologue**, experiments with time, myth, symbol.
- Other modern names: **T. S. Eliot** (*The Waste Land*, 1922), **W. B. Yeats**, **E. M. Forster** (*A Passage to India*, 1924), **Aldous Huxley** (*Brave New World*, 1932).

## James Joyce (1882–1941), Irish 🔥
| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| ***Dubliners*** | 1914 | 15 short stories; "paralysis" of Dublin life; last story "The Dead" |
| ***A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man*** | 1916 | Autobiographical; hero **Stephen Dedalus** |
| ***Ulysses*** 🔥 | **1922** | Modelled on Homer's *Odyssey*; set in Dublin on **16 June 1904** ("**Bloomsday**"); **Leopold Bloom**, **Molly Bloom**, Stephen Dedalus; ends with Molly's unpunctuated monologue |
| ***Finnegans Wake*** | 1939 | Most experimental; dream language |
| *Exiles* (play), *Chamber Music* (poems) | 1918, 1907 | Minor works |

- Joyce used **epiphany**: a sudden moment of spiritual insight.
- *Ulysses* is often called the greatest novel of the 20th century; it was banned for obscenity in the USA and UK for years.

## Virginia Woolf (1882–1941), English 🔥
- Leading member of the **Bloomsbury Group**; with her husband Leonard Woolf she ran the **Hogarth Press**.
- She drowned herself in the **River Ouse** in 1941.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| *The Voyage Out* | 1915 | First novel |
| *Jacob's Room* | 1922 | |
| ***Mrs Dalloway*** 🔥 | **1925** | One day in London; **Clarissa Dalloway** and shell-shocked **Septimus Warren Smith** |
| ***To the Lighthouse*** 🔥 | **1927** | **Mrs Ramsay**, painter **Lily Briscoe**; three parts: "The Window", "Time Passes", "The Lighthouse" |
| *Orlando* | 1928 | Hero lives for centuries and changes sex |
| ***A Room of One's Own*** | **1929** | Feminist essay: "A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." Invents **Judith Shakespeare** |
| *The Waves* | 1931 | Six voices in soliloquies |
| *Between the Acts* | 1941 | Last novel |

- Essay "Modern Fiction" attacks the "materialists" (Wells, Bennett, Galsworthy).

## D. H. Lawrence (1885–1930), English
- Son of a Nottinghamshire coal miner; wrote about sex, instinct and industrial society.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| *The White Peacock* | 1911 | First novel |
| ***Sons and Lovers*** 🔥 | **1913** | Autobiographical; **Paul Morel**, mother **Gertrude Morel**, **Miriam**, **Clara**; mother–son bond (Oedipal theme) |
| ***The Rainbow*** | 1915 | Three generations of the **Brangwen** family; banned for obscenity |
| ***Women in Love*** | 1920 | Sisters **Ursula** and **Gudrun Brangwen** |
| ***Lady Chatterley's Lover*** | **1928** | **Constance (Connie) Chatterley** and gamekeeper **Oliver Mellors**; full text published in the UK only after the **1960** Penguin obscenity trial |
| Poems | | "**Snake**", "**Piano**", "**Bavarian Gentians**" |

## Joseph Conrad (1857–1924), Polish-born British 🔥
- Real name **Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski**. He was a sailor and learned English as an adult, yet became a master of English prose.
- Narrator **Charles Marlow** appears in *Heart of Darkness*, *Lord Jim*, *Youth* and *Chance*.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| *Almayer's Folly* | 1895 | First novel |
| *The Nigger of the 'Narcissus'* | 1897 | Preface: "to make you see" |
| ***Heart of Darkness*** 🔥 | **1899** (book 1902) | Marlow's voyage up the **Congo** river to find **Kurtz**, an ivory trader; Kurtz's last words: "**The horror! The horror!**" |
| ***Lord Jim*** | 1900 | Jim abandons the ship *Patna*; lifelong search for redemption |
| ***Nostromo*** | 1904 | Imaginary South American republic Costaguana; silver mine |
| *The Secret Agent* | 1907 | Anarchists in London; **Verloc** |
| *Under Western Eyes* | 1911 | Russian revolutionaries |
| *Victory* | 1915 | |

- **Chinua Achebe** called Conrad "a thoroughgoing racist" in his lecture "**An Image of Africa**" (1975).

## George Orwell (1903–1950), English 🔥🔥
- Real name **Eric Arthur Blair**; born at **Motihari, Bihar, India**. Served in the Indian Imperial Police in **Burma**.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| *Down and Out in Paris and London* | 1933 | First book; poverty |
| *Burmese Days* | 1934 | Colonial Burma |
| *The Road to Wigan Pier* | 1937 | Working-class life in northern England |
| *Homage to Catalonia* | 1938 | Spanish Civil War |
| ***Animal Farm*** 🔥 | **1945** | Subtitle "**A Fairy Story**"; allegory of the **Russian Revolution** and Stalinism |
| ***Nineteen Eighty-Four*** 🔥 | **1949** | Dystopia; state **Oceania**; ruler **Big Brother** |
| Essays | | "**Shooting an Elephant**", "Politics and the English Language", "Why I Write" |

**Animal Farm:** **Old Major** (idea of rebellion; Marx/Lenin), **Napoleon** (Stalin), **Snowball** (Trotsky), **Squealer** (propaganda), **Boxer** (loyal cart-horse; motto "I will work harder"), **Benjamin** (cynical donkey), **Mollie**, **Mr Jones** (the farmer).
- "**All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.**"
- "Four legs good, two legs bad."

**Nineteen Eighty-Four:** **Winston Smith**, **Julia**, **O'Brien**, **Emmanuel Goldstein**; **Thought Police**, **Newspeak**, **doublethink**, **Room 101**, Ministry of Truth.
- "**Big Brother is watching you.**"
- Party slogans: "**War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.**"
- The adjective **"Orwellian"** means a totalitarian, surveillance-driven state.

## Quick revision
- Stream of consciousness: **Joyce, Woolf**; term from **William James**.
- *Ulysses* (1922) = **Leopold Bloom**, one day, **16 June 1904**.
- *Mrs Dalloway* (1925), *To the Lighthouse* (1927), *A Room of One's Own* (1929): **Woolf**.
- *Sons and Lovers* (1913), **Paul Morel**: **Lawrence**.
- *Heart of Darkness*: **Marlow, Kurtz, Congo**; "The horror! The horror!"
- Conrad's real name: **Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski**.
- Orwell = **Eric Arthur Blair**, born in **India** (Motihari).
- *Animal Farm* (1945) = allegory of the **Russian Revolution**; *1984* (1949) = **Big Brother**.

ENG-29.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Almost every BCS, bank and NTRCA paper has one or two "fill in the gap" or "choose the correct form" questions on *if*-clauses, *unless*, inverted conditionals ("Had I known…") and *wish / as if / it is time*.

## The four main types 🔥
| Type | Use | *If*-clause | Main clause | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Zero** | General truths, facts | present simple | present simple | If you **heat** ice, it **melts**. |
| **First** | Real / likely future | present simple | **will / can / may + V1** | If it **rains**, we **will stay** at home. |
| **Second** | Unreal present or unlikely future | past simple (**were** for all persons) | **would / could / might + V1** | If I **were** a bird, I **would fly**. |
| **Third** | Unreal past (did not happen) | **had + V3** | **would / could / might have + V3** | If he **had worked** hard, he **would have passed**. |

**Memory hook:** *Present → will; Past → would; Past perfect → would have.*

## Key rules 🔥
1. **No *will* in the *if*-clause** of a first conditional. ✗ If it *will rain*… ✓ If it **rains**…
2. **"Were" for all persons** in the second conditional: *If I were you, I would not go.* ("If I was" is informal and marked wrong in exams.)
3. **Third conditional never takes *would* in the *if*-clause.** ✗ If he *would have come*… ✓ If he **had come**…
4. **Unless = if … not.** Do not use *not* again after *unless*.
   - ✓ **Unless you work hard, you will fail.** ✗ Unless you do not work hard…
5. A comma is used when the *if*-clause comes first: *If you call me, I will come.* / *I will come if you call me.*

## Inverted conditionals (without *if*) 🔥
| With *if* | Inverted form |
|---|---|
| If I had known the truth, I would have helped. | **Had I known** the truth, I would have helped. |
| If I were rich, I would buy a car. | **Were I** rich, I would buy a car. |
| If you should need help, call me. | **Should you need** help, call me. |

Exam trap: "**Had** I been a king, I **would have** built…" (not "would build") when the meaning is past.

## Mixed conditionals
| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| Past condition → present result | If I **had taken** the medicine, I **would be** well **now**. |
| Present condition → past result | If I **were** a good swimmer, I **would have saved** the boy yesterday. |

## Other words that introduce a condition
| Word | Example |
|---|---|
| **provided (that) / providing** | You may go **provided** you finish the work. |
| **as long as / so long as** | You can stay **as long as** you keep quiet. |
| **on condition that** | He was released **on condition that** he left the country. |
| **in case** (precaution) | Take an umbrella **in case** it rains. |
| **suppose / supposing** | **Suppose** you lost your job, what would you do? |
| **but for / without + noun** | **But for** your help, I **would have failed**. |
| **otherwise / or else** | Hurry up, **otherwise** you will miss the bus. |
| **even if** | I will go **even if** it rains. |

## Related "unreal" structures 🔥
| Structure | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **I wish** (present) | wish + past / were | I wish I **were** a king. I wish I **knew** his address. |
| **I wish** (past) | wish + had + V3 | I wish I **had seen** the match. |
| **I wish** (future / annoyance) | wish + would | I wish you **would stop** talking. |
| **as if / as though** | + past / were (unreal) | He talks **as if** he **were** the boss. |
| | + had + V3 (past) | He looked **as if** he **had seen** a ghost. |
| **It is (high / about) time** | + subject + past | **It is high time** we **left**. / It is time you **went** to bed. |
| **would rather** (someone else) | + subject + past | I **would rather** you **stayed** here. |
| **If only** | same as *wish* | **If only** I **had listened** to you! |

## Worked examples
1. If I ____ you, I would accept the offer. → **were** (second conditional).
2. If he had run fast, he ____ the train. → **would have caught** (third).
3. ____ harder, he would have won. → **Had he tried** (inversion of third).
4. Unless you ____, you will be late. → **hurry** (not "do not hurry").
5. If water ____ to 100°C, it boils. → **is heated** (zero conditional, fact).

## Quick revision
- First: **If + present, will + V1**.
- Second: **If + past (were), would + V1**.
- Third: **If + had + V3, would have + V3**.
- **Unless = if not**; never "unless … not".
- **Had I known = If I had known**; **Were I = If I were**; **Should you = If you should**.
- **It is high time + past**: It is high time we started.
- **I wish + were / had + V3**.
- **But for** + noun = if it had not been for.

ENG-30.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who wrote a play, which play a character belongs to, the subtitle of a play, and labels such as "Theatre of the Absurd", "Angry Young Men" and "comedy of manners".

## George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950), Irish 🔥
- Nobel Prize in Literature **1925**. He also won an **Academy Award (Oscar)** for the screenplay of *Pygmalion* (1938 film). He is often cited as the **first person to win both a Nobel and an Oscar** (Bob Dylan later did both too).
- Member of the socialist **Fabian Society**. Admirer of Ibsen: wrote ***The Quintessence of Ibsenism*** (1891).
- Known for the **drama of ideas / discussion play**, long prefaces, wit. Adjective: **Shavian**.

| Play | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| *Widowers' Houses* | 1892 | First play; slum landlords |
| *Mrs Warren's Profession* | 1893 | Prostitution; long banned |
| ***Arms and the Man*** 🔥 | **1894** | Anti-romantic view of war; Swiss soldier **Bluntschli**, the "**chocolate cream soldier**"; **Raina**, **Sergius**. Title from the opening of Virgil's *Aeneid* ("Arms and the man I sing") |
| *Candida* | 1894 | |
| *Caesar and Cleopatra* | 1898 | |
| ***Man and Superman*** | **1903** | **John Tanner**, **Ann Whitefield**; the "**Life Force**"; "Don Juan in Hell" dream scene. Its "Maxims for Revolutionists" contain: "He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches." |
| ***Major Barbara*** | 1905 | Salvation Army officer Barbara vs her arms-maker father **Andrew Undershaft** |
| *The Doctor's Dilemma* | 1906 | |
| ***Pygmalion*** 🔥 | **1913** | Phonetics professor **Henry Higgins** trains flower girl **Eliza Doolittle**; **Colonel Pickering**; Eliza's father **Alfred Doolittle**. Basis of the musical ***My Fair Lady*** |
| *Heartbreak House* | 1919 | |
| ***Saint Joan*** | **1923** | Joan of Arc; led to his Nobel recognition |
| *The Apple Cart* | 1929 | |

## Oscar Wilde (1854–1900), Irish 🔥
- Leader of **Aestheticism**: "**Art for art's sake**". Famous for epigrams and the **comedy of manners**.
- Jailed in **1895** for "gross indecency"; in prison he wrote the long letter ***De Profundis***; later the poem ***The Ballad of Reading Gaol*** (1898). He died in Paris in 1900.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Picture of Dorian Gray*** | 1890 (book 1891) | His **only novel**; **Dorian Gray** stays young while his portrait ages; painter **Basil Hallward**, **Lord Henry Wotton** |
| *Lady Windermere's Fan* | 1892 | "I can resist everything except temptation." |
| *Salomé* | 1891 (written in **French**) | One-act tragedy |
| *A Woman of No Importance* | 1893 | |
| *An Ideal Husband* | 1895 | |
| ***The Importance of Being Earnest*** 🔥 | **1895** | Subtitle "**A Trivial Comedy for Serious People**"; **Jack (John) Worthing**, **Algernon Moncrieff**, **Gwendolen Fairfax**, **Cecily Cardew**, **Lady Bracknell**, **Miss Prism**; pun on "Earnest / Ernest"; the "Bunburying" joke |
| Fairy tales | 1888, 1891 | ***The Happy Prince***, *The Selfish Giant*, *The Nightingale and the Rose* |

## Samuel Beckett (1906–1989), Irish 🔥
- Lived in Paris; wrote in **French and English**. Nobel Prize in Literature **1969**.
- Leading dramatist of the **Theatre of the Absurd**. The term was coined by critic **Martin Esslin** (book, 1961). Absurd drama shows the meaninglessness of life, with little plot, circular action and broken language.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| ***Waiting for Godot*** 🔥 | French *En attendant Godot* staged **1953**; English 1955 | Subtitle "**a tragicomedy in two acts**"; tramps **Vladimir (Didi)** and **Estragon (Gogo)** wait for Godot, who never comes; **Pozzo** and his slave **Lucky**; a Boy. Opening line: "**Nothing to be done.**" Critic Vivian Mercier: a play in which "nothing happens, twice" |
| ***Endgame*** | 1957 | **Hamm**, **Clov**, **Nagg**, **Nell** (parents in dustbins) |
| *Krapp's Last Tape* | 1958 | Old man and his tape recorder |
| *Happy Days* | 1961 | **Winnie** buried in a mound; **Willie** |
| Novels | 1938–1953 | *Murphy*; trilogy *Molloy*, *Malone Dies*, *The Unnamable* |

Other absurdists: **Eugène Ionesco** (*The Bald Soprano*, *Rhinoceros*), **Jean Genet**, **Harold Pinter** ("comedy of menace": *The Birthday Party*, *The Caretaker*, *The Homecoming*; Nobel 2005), **Edward Albee** (*The Zoo Story*).

## John Osborne (1929–1994), English 🔥
- ***Look Back in Anger*** (**1956**, **Royal Court Theatre**, London) changed post-war British theatre.
- Characters: **Jimmy Porter** (angry, working-class, university-educated), his wife **Alison**, friend **Cliff Lewis**, actress **Helena Charles**, Alison's father **Colonel Redfern**; the couple's "**bears and squirrels**" game.
- It began the "**Angry Young Men**" label and "**kitchen sink drama**" (realistic drama of ordinary working-class homes).
- Other plays: ***The Entertainer*** (1957, Archie Rice), ***Luther*** (1961), *Inadmissible Evidence* (1964).
- Other "Angry Young Men": **Kingsley Amis** (*Lucky Jim*, 1954), **John Wain**, **John Braine** (*Room at the Top*), **Alan Sillitoe**, **Arnold Wesker**.

## Other modern drama names often asked
| Dramatist | Play |
|---|---|
| **T. S. Eliot** | ***Murder in the Cathedral*** (1935, verse drama on Thomas Becket) |
| **J. M. Synge** | ***Riders to the Sea*** (1904), *The Playboy of the Western World* (1907) |
| **Sean O'Casey** | *Juno and the Paycock* (1924) |
| **Henrik Ibsen** (Norway) | *A Doll's House* (1879), father of modern (realist) drama |

## Quick revision
- *Arms and the Man*, *Pygmalion*, *Man and Superman*, *Saint Joan*: **Shaw** (Nobel 1925).
- "Chocolate cream soldier" = **Bluntschli**.
- *Pygmalion* → musical **My Fair Lady**; **Eliza Doolittle, Henry Higgins**.
- *The Importance of Being Earnest* (1895): "A Trivial Comedy for Serious People": **Wilde**.
- Wilde's only novel: ***The Picture of Dorian Gray***.
- *Waiting for Godot*: **Vladimir, Estragon, Pozzo, Lucky**; **Theatre of the Absurd** (term: **Martin Esslin**).
- *Look Back in Anger* (1956): **Jimmy Porter**; "**Angry Young Men**", **kitchen sink drama**.

ENG-31.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Every BCS and bank paper has "Which sentence is correct?" or "Find the error" questions. The same 50 or so traps repeat: subject–verb agreement, uncountable nouns, wrong prepositions, tense with *since/for*, and redundancy.

## 1. Subject–verb agreement 🔥
| Incorrect | Correct | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| One of my friend is a doctor. | One of my **friends is** a doctor. | *one of* + plural noun + singular verb |
| Each of the boys have a pen. | Each of the boys **has** a pen. | *each, every, either, neither* → singular |
| The Principal, along with the teachers, were present. | … **was** present. | *along with, as well as, with, together with* do not change the subject |
| Neither he nor I are guilty. | Neither he nor I **am** guilty. | *either/neither … or/nor*: verb agrees with the **nearer** subject |
| A number of students is absent. | A number of students **are** absent. | *a number of* = many → plural |
| The number of students are fifty. | The number of students **is** fifty. | *the number of* → singular |
| The cattle is grazing. | The cattle **are** grazing. | *cattle, police, people, poultry, gentry* → always plural |
| The police has arrested him. | The police **have** arrested him. | same rule |
| Mathematics are my favourite subject. | Mathematics **is** … | *mathematics, physics, economics, news* → singular |
| The news are true. | The news **is** true. | |
| Twenty miles are a long distance. | Twenty miles **is** a long distance. | amount/distance as one unit → singular |
| The rich is not always happy. | The rich **are** … | *the + adjective* = plural class |
| He is one of the best boys who **has** passed. | … who **have** passed. | *one of those who* → plural verb (exam answer) |

## 2. Nouns: uncountable words 🔥
Words that **never take -s or "a/an"**: *advice, information, furniture, luggage, baggage, scenery, machinery, poetry, equipment, bread, mischief*, and *hair* (meaning all the hair on the head).
| Incorrect | Correct |
|---|---|
| He gave me an advice. | He gave me **some advice / a piece of advice**. |
| I need some informations. | I need some **information**. |
| The sceneries of Cox's Bazar are charming. | The **scenery** of Cox's Bazar **is** charming. |
| My luggages are lost. | My **luggage is** lost. |
| He bought new furnitures. | He bought new **furniture**. |
| His hairs are grey. | His **hair is** grey. |

## 3. Pronouns
| Incorrect | Correct | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Between you and I | Between you and **me** | object after preposition |
| Let he go. | Let **him** go. | object after *let* |
| He is taller than me. (formal test) | He is taller than **I** (am). | exam prefers subjective case after *than* |
| I and you will go. | **You and I** will go. | order: 2nd, 3rd, 1st person (for good things) |
| One should do his duty. | One should do **one's** duty. | *one → one's* |
| Everyone of them | **Every one** of them | *every one* (two words) before *of* |

## 4. Tense errors 🔥
| Incorrect | Correct | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| He has been ill since three days. | He has been ill **for** three days. | *for* + period; *since* + point of time |
| I am living here since 2010. | I **have been living** here since 2010. | *since* → present perfect (continuous) |
| I have seen him yesterday. | I **saw** him yesterday. | past time word → past simple |
| He did not came. | He did not **come**. | *did* + V1 |
| Have you ever went there? | Have you ever **gone** there? | *have* + V3 |
| No sooner had he come **when** I left. | No sooner had he come **than** I left. | *no sooner … than* |
| Hardly had he gone **than** it rained. | Hardly had he gone **when** it rained. | *hardly/scarcely … when/before* |
| If I was you… | If I **were** you… | unreal condition |
| Walk fast lest you **should not** miss the bus. | … lest you **should** miss the bus. | *lest* already means "so that not" |

## 5. Adjectives & comparison 🔥
| Incorrect | Correct |
|---|---|
| He is senior **than** me. | He is senior **to** me. (*senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior, prefer* → *to*) |
| I prefer tea **than** coffee. | I prefer tea **to** coffee. |
| This is **more better**. | This is **better**. (no double comparative) |
| She is the **most perfect** lady. | She is a **perfect** lady. (*perfect, unique, ideal, round* have no comparison) |
| His house is bigger than **me**. | His house is bigger than **mine**. |
| He is one of the tallest **boy**. | … one of the tallest **boys**. |
| He is **a** honest man. | He is **an** honest man. (sound, not letter) |
| He studies in **an** university. | … in **a** university. ("yu" sound) |

## 6. Preposition errors 🔥
| Incorrect | Correct |
|---|---|
| He died **from** cholera. | He died **of** cholera. (disease → *of*) |
| She is married **with** a doctor. | She is married **to** a doctor. |
| He is good **in** English. | He is good **at** English. |
| He is blind **from** one eye. | He is blind **of** one eye. |
| I am angry **on** him. | I am angry **with** him (person) / **at** his conduct (thing). |
| He congratulated me **for** my success. | … **on** my success. |
| He is fond **with** music. | He is fond **of** music. |
| Listen me. | Listen **to** me. |

## 7. Redundancy (extra words) 🔥
| Incorrect | Correct |
|---|---|
| Let us **discuss about** it. | Let us **discuss** it. |
| He **returned back**. | He **returned**. |
| **Cope up with** | **Cope with** |
| **Order for** a book | **Order** a book |
| **Repeat again** | **Repeat** |
| **Though** he is poor, **but** he is honest. | Though he is poor, he is honest. (or *yet*) |
| **Both** Rahim **as well as** Karim | **Both** Rahim **and** Karim |
| **Unless** you **do not** work hard… | **Unless** you work hard… |
| The **reason** is **because**… | The reason is **that**… |

## 8. Verb patterns (gerund / infinitive)
| Incorrect | Correct |
|---|---|
| He made me **to cry**. | He made me **cry**. (*make, let, see, hear* + bare infinitive) |
| Would you mind **to open** the door? | Would you mind **opening** the door? |
| I look forward to **meet** you. | I look forward to **meeting** you. |
| He avoided **to meet** me. | He avoided **meeting** me. |
| He enjoyed during the holidays. | He **enjoyed himself** during the holidays. |

## Quick revision
- **One of + plural noun + singular verb.**
- **Cattle, police, people** → plural; **news, mathematics** → singular.
- **Advice, information, furniture, scenery, luggage** → no plural.
- **Since** + point, **for** + period; *since* → present perfect.
- **Senior/junior/superior/prefer + to**, not *than*.
- **Died of** a disease; **married to**; **good at**.
- **Discuss** (no *about*); **return** (no *back*); **cope with** (no *up*).
- **No sooner … than**; **Hardly/Scarcely … when**.
