ENG-32.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask who wrote a poem, novel or play, famous lines ("The woods are lovely, dark and deep…"), characters (Santiago, Willy Loman), and epithets such as "father of free verse".

## Walt Whitman (1819–1892) 🔥
- Called the **father of free verse** and the "**Bard of Democracy**".
- ***Leaves of Grass*** (**1855**; he kept revising and enlarging it until 1892). Main poem: "**Song of Myself**", which opens "**I celebrate myself, and sing myself**".

| Poem | Key points |
|---|---|
| "**O Captain! My Captain!**" 🔥 | **Elegy on Abraham Lincoln** (1865); the "Captain" = Lincoln, the "ship" = the nation after the Civil War |
| "**When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd**" | Also an elegy for **Lincoln** |
| "I Hear America Singing" | Workers of America |
| "Crossing Brooklyn Ferry", "Passage to India" | |
| *Drum-Taps* (1865) | Civil War poems |

## Robert Frost (1874–1963) 🔥
- Poet of rural **New England**; won the **Pulitzer Prize four times** (a record for poetry).
- Recited "**The Gift Outright**" at **John F. Kennedy's inauguration (1961)**.
- Collections: ***A Boy's Will*** (1913, first), ***North of Boston*** (1914), *Mountain Interval* (1916), *New Hampshire* (1923).

| Poem | Famous lines |
|---|---|
| "**Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening**" 🔥 | "**The woods are lovely, dark and deep, / But I have promises to keep, / And miles to go before I sleep**" (Nehru kept these lines on his desk) |
| "**The Road Not Taken**" 🔥 | "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood… **I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference.**" |
| "**Mending Wall**" | "**Good fences make good neighbors**"; "Something there is that doesn't love a wall" |
| "Birches", "After Apple-Picking" | |
| "**Fire and Ice**" | "Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice" |
| "The Death of the Hired Man", "Home Burial" | Dramatic narratives |
| "Nothing Gold Can Stay" | |

## Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) 🔥🔥
- Nobel Prize in Literature **1954**; Pulitzer Prize **1953** for *The Old Man and the Sea*.
- Style: short, plain sentences; the "**iceberg theory**" (theory of omission). Member of the "**Lost Generation**" (Gertrude Stein's phrase). He died by suicide in 1961.

| Work | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Sun Also Rises*** | 1926 | **Jake Barnes**, **Lady Brett Ashley**; epigraph "You are all a lost generation" |
| ***A Farewell to Arms*** | **1929** | WWI Italy; **Frederic Henry** and nurse **Catherine Barkley** |
| *To Have and Have Not* | 1937 | |
| ***For Whom the Bell Tolls*** | **1940** | **Spanish Civil War**; **Robert Jordan**, **Maria**; title from **John Donne**'s *Meditation XVII* |
| ***The Old Man and the Sea*** 🔥 | **1952** | Cuban fisherman **Santiago**, the boy **Manolin**, a giant **marlin**, sharks. "**A man can be destroyed but not defeated.**" |
| Short stories | | "**The Snows of Kilimanjaro**", "The Killers", "Hills Like White Elephants" |
| *A Moveable Feast* | 1964 (posthumous) | Memoir of Paris in the 1920s |

## Arthur Miller (1915–2005) 🔥
- Leading American playwright; wrote the essay "**Tragedy and the Common Man**" (1949): a common man can be a tragic hero. Was married to **Marilyn Monroe** (1956–1961).

| Play | Year | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| ***All My Sons*** | 1947 | **Joe Keller** sold faulty aircraft parts in WWII |
| ***Death of a Salesman*** 🔥 | **1949** | **Pulitzer Prize**; **Willy Loman** (the failing salesman), wife **Linda**, sons **Biff** and **Happy**; the "American Dream". Linda: "**Attention must be paid.**" |
| ***The Crucible*** 🔥 | **1953** | **Salem witch trials** (1692) used as an **allegory of McCarthyism**; **John Proctor**, **Abigail Williams** |
| *A View from the Bridge* | 1955 | Eddie Carbone |
| *After the Fall*, *The Price* | 1964, 1968 | |

## Other American writers often asked
| Writer | Famous work / fact |
|---|---|
| **Nathaniel Hawthorne** | ***The Scarlet Letter*** (1850): **Hester Prynne**, letter "A" |
| **Herman Melville** | ***Moby-Dick*** (1851): **Captain Ahab**, white whale; "Call me Ishmael" |
| **Edgar Allan Poe** | "The Raven"; father of the detective story ("The Murders in the Rue Morgue") |
| **Mark Twain** (Samuel L. Clemens) | ***Adventures of Huckleberry Finn*** (1884), *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer* |
| **Emily Dickinson** | Short untitled lyrics; "Because I could not stop for Death" |
| **Harriet Beecher Stowe** | ***Uncle Tom's Cabin*** (1852), anti-slavery novel |
| **F. Scott Fitzgerald** | ***The Great Gatsby*** (1925): **Jay Gatsby**, Nick Carraway |
| **William Faulkner** | *The Sound and the Fury*; Nobel **1949** |
| **John Steinbeck** | ***The Grapes of Wrath*** (1939), *Of Mice and Men*; Nobel **1962** |
| **Eugene O'Neill** | *Long Day's Journey into Night*, *The Emperor Jones*; Nobel **1936** (the only American dramatist to win it) |
| **Tennessee Williams** | ***A Streetcar Named Desire*** (1947, Blanche DuBois), *The Glass Menagerie* |
| **Sinclair Lewis** | *Main Street*, *Babbitt*; **first American Nobel laureate in literature (1930)** |
| **Harper Lee** | ***To Kill a Mockingbird*** (1960): Atticus Finch |
| **Toni Morrison** | ***Beloved*** (1987); Nobel **1993** |
| **H. W. Longfellow** | "A Psalm of Life", *Evangeline* |
| **R. W. Emerson / H. D. Thoreau** | Transcendentalism; Thoreau's ***Walden*** (1854) |

## Quick revision
- *Leaves of Grass* (1855): **Whitman**, father of free verse.
- "O Captain! My Captain!": elegy on **Abraham Lincoln**.
- "Miles to go before I sleep": **Frost**, "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening".
- "Good fences make good neighbors": **Frost**, "Mending Wall".
- *The Old Man and the Sea* (1952): **Santiago**; Hemingway Nobel **1954**.
- *For Whom the Bell Tolls*: **Spanish Civil War**; title from **John Donne**.
- *Death of a Salesman* (1949): **Willy Loman**.
- *The Crucible* (1953): Salem witch trials = **McCarthyism**.

ENG-33.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Job exams give the first half of a sentence ("No sooner had he reached the station…") or a gap, and you choose the correct ending. Most items test a **fixed structure**, so learning the patterns below solves most of them quickly.

## How to solve
1. Find the **signal word** (no sooner, lest, too, unless, wish, as if, it is time, though…).
2. Check **tense agreement** between the two parts.
3. Check the **logic** (cause–effect, contrast, condition).
4. Remove options with **double negatives** or **redundancy**.

## Fixed patterns 🔥
| Beginning / signal | Correct completion | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **No sooner had** + subject + V3 | **than** + past | No sooner had he reached the station **than the train left**. |
| **Hardly / Scarcely had** + subject + V3 | **when / before** + past | Hardly had we started **when it began to rain**. |
| **Lest** | **should** + V1 (no *not*) | Walk carefully lest you **should fall**. |
| **too … to** | V1 (no *not*) | He is too weak **to walk**. |
| **so … that** | clause with *can't / couldn't* | He is so weak **that he cannot walk**. |
| **Though / Although** | no *but* in the main clause (*yet* is allowed) | Though he is poor, **he is honest**. |
| **Not only … but also** | parallel parts | She is not only beautiful **but also intelligent**. |
| **Either … or / Neither … nor** | nearer subject decides verb | Neither the teacher nor the students **were** present. |
| **Unless** | positive verb | Unless you hurry, **you will miss the bus**. |
| **If** + present | **will** + V1 | If you work hard, **you will succeed**. |
| **If** + past | **would** + V1 | If I were rich, **I would help the poor**. |
| **If** + had + V3 | **would have** + V3 | If he had come, **I would have met him**. |
| **It is (high) time** | subject + past | It is high time **we left**. |
| **I wish** | past / had + V3 | I wish **I were a bird**. |
| **As if / As though** | were / had + V3 | He behaves as if **he were a king**. |
| **Would rather … than** | V1 … V1 | I would rather **die than beg**. |
| **Had better** | V1 (no *to*) | You had better **consult a doctor**. |
| **Since** (time) | present perfect in main clause | It **has been** five years since **he left**. |
| **Used to** + V1 | past habit | He used to **smoke**, but now he doesn't. |
| **Be used to / accustomed to** + V-ing | present habit | I am used to **walking** long distances. |
| **Look forward to / object to / with a view to** | V-ing | I look forward to **hearing** from you. |
| **It is no use / worth / can't help** | V-ing | It is no use **crying** over spilt milk. |
| **Make / let / see / hear** + object | bare V1 | He made me **laugh**. |
| **Until / till** | positive verb | Wait here until **I return**. |
| **Before / after / when** (future) | present tense in time clause | I will call you when **he comes**. |
| **The + comparative …, the + comparative** | | The more you read, **the more you learn**. |
| **Such … that / So … that** | result | It was such a hot day **that we stayed indoors**. |
| **In order that / so that** | may / might / can | He works hard so that **he may succeed**. |
| **Whether … or** | or (not *if … or*) | I don't know whether he will come **or not**. |
| **Both … and** | and (not *as well as*) | Both Rina **and Mina** passed. |
| **Prefer … to** | to + noun / V-ing | I prefer tea **to coffee**. |
| **Prefer to V1 … rather than V1** | | I prefer to walk **rather than ride**. |

## Tense matching tips
- Past in the first part → usually past in the second: *He said that he **was** ill.*
- Universal truth stays present even after a past verb: *The teacher said that the earth **moves** round the sun.*
- **By the time** + past → past perfect: *By the time the doctor came, the patient **had died**.*
- **By the time** + present → future perfect: *By the time you arrive, I **will have left**.*

## Logic-based completions
| Beginning | Logical ending |
|---|---|
| He is honest; **therefore** … | everybody trusts him. |
| He was ill; **nevertheless** … | he attended the meeting. |
| **Because** it was raining, … | the match was postponed. |
| **In spite of** his illness, … | he went to the office. (*in spite of / despite* + noun or V-ing) |
| **As** he was late, … | he missed the train. |

## Quick revision
- **No sooner … than**; **Hardly / Scarcely … when**.
- **Lest … should** (never *should not*).
- **Too … to** has a negative meaning; do not add *not*.
- **Though** does not take *but*.
- **It is high time + past**; **I wish + were**; **had better + V1**.
- **Look forward to + V-ing**; **used to + V1**; **be used to + V-ing**.
- **By the time + past → had + V3**.

ENG-34.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask definitions ("A sonnet has how many lines?"), forms (Petrarchan vs Shakespearean), and famous examples ("*Lycidas* is a…", "*Adonais* is written on…").

## Sonnet 🔥🔥
- A poem of **14 lines**, usually in **iambic pentameter**. From Italian *sonetto* = "little song".
- Perfected by the Italian poet **Petrarch** (poems to **Laura**).
- Introduced into English by **Sir Thomas Wyatt**; the **Earl of Surrey** developed the English form (Surrey also first used **blank verse** in English).
- **Volta** = the "turn" in thought (usually at line 9 in the Petrarchan sonnet).

| Type | Structure | Rhyme scheme | Poets |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Petrarchan / Italian** | **Octave (8) + sestet (6)** | abbaabba + cdecde or cdcdcd | Petrarch, **Milton**, Wordsworth |
| **Shakespearean / English** | **3 quatrains + a couplet** | **abab cdcd efef gg** | Shakespeare |
| **Spenserian** | 3 linked quatrains + couplet | abab bcbc cdcd ee | Spenser (*Amoretti*) |

| Sonnet sequence / sonnet | Poet |
|---|---|
| **154 sonnets** (1609); Sonnet 18 "**Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?**"; "Fair Youth", "Dark Lady" | **Shakespeare** |
| ***Astrophel and Stella*** | **Sir Philip Sidney** |
| ***Amoretti*** | **Edmund Spenser** |
| "**On His Blindness**" ("They also serve who only stand and wait") | **Milton** |
| "**Death, be not proud**" (Holy Sonnets) | **John Donne** |
| "The world is too much with us", "Composed upon Westminster Bridge", "London, 1802" | **Wordsworth** |
| "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer", "Bright star" | **Keats** |
| "**Ozymandias**" | **Shelley** |
| ***Sonnets from the Portuguese*** ("How do I love thee? Let me count the ways") | **Elizabeth Barrett Browning** |

Bangla note: **Michael Madhusudan Dutt** introduced the sonnet (চতুর্দশপদী কবিতা) into Bangla.

## Ode 🔥
- A long, serious **lyric poem in an elevated style**, usually **addressed** to a person, object or idea.

| Type | Features |
|---|---|
| **Pindaric** | From Greek poet **Pindar**; strophe, antistrophe, epode |
| **Horatian** | From Latin poet **Horace**; regular stanzas, calm tone |
| **Irregular** | Free stanza lengths (Abraham **Cowley**, Wordsworth's *Immortality Ode*) |

| Ode | Poet | Famous line |
|---|---|---|
| "**Ode to a Nightingale**" (1819) | **Keats** | "My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains"; "Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!" |
| "**Ode on a Grecian Urn**" (1819) | **Keats** | "**Beauty is truth, truth beauty**"; "Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter" |
| "**To Autumn**" (1819) | **Keats** | "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness" |
| "Ode on Melancholy", "Ode to Psyche" | Keats | |
| "**Ode to the West Wind**" (1819) | **Shelley** | "**If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?**" |
| "**Ode: Intimations of Immortality**" | **Wordsworth** | Epigraph: "The Child is father of the Man" |
| "Dejection: An Ode" | Coleridge | |
| "Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College" | **Thomas Gray** | "where ignorance is bliss, / 'Tis folly to be wise" |

## Elegy 🔥
- A poem of **mourning for the dead** (or a serious meditation on death).
- **Pastoral elegy:** the poet and the dead person appear as shepherds.

| Elegy | Poet | Mourns |
|---|---|---|
| ***Lycidas*** (1637) 🔥 | **Milton** | His college friend **Edward King** (drowned) |
| ***Adonais*** (1821) 🔥 | **Shelley** | **John Keats** |
| ***Thyrsis*** | **Matthew Arnold** | Poet **Arthur Hugh Clough** |
| ***In Memoriam A.H.H.*** (1850) 🔥 | **Tennyson** | Friend **Arthur Henry Hallam**; "'Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all"; "Nature, red in tooth and claw" |
| "**Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard**" (1751) 🔥 | **Thomas Gray** | Humble villagers; "The paths of glory lead but to the grave"; "Full many a flower is born to blush unseen" |
| "**O Captain! My Captain!**" | **Walt Whitman** | **Abraham Lincoln** |
| "In Memory of W. B. Yeats" | W. H. Auden | Yeats |
| "Do not go gentle into that good night" | Dylan Thomas | His dying father (a **villanelle**) |

## Epic 🔥
- A **long narrative poem** on heroic deeds, in an **elevated style**, with a hero of national importance, supernatural forces, an **invocation to the Muse**, starting ***in medias res*** ("in the middle of things"), and **epic (Homeric) similes**.
- **Primary / folk epic:** grows from oral tradition (*Iliad*, *Beowulf*). **Secondary / literary epic:** written by one poet in imitation (*Aeneid*, *Paradise Lost*).

| Epic | Poet / origin |
|---|---|
| ***Iliad*** (Trojan War, Achilles), ***Odyssey*** (Odysseus) | **Homer** (Greek) |
| ***Aeneid*** (Aeneas) | **Virgil** (Latin) |
| ***Beowulf*** | Anonymous; **oldest epic in English** (Old English) |
| ***The Divine Comedy*** | **Dante** (Italian) |
| ***The Faerie Queene*** (unfinished; for Elizabeth I) | **Edmund Spenser** |
| ***Paradise Lost*** (1667; 12 books in the 1674 edition; blank verse; "justify the ways of God to men") 🔥 | **John Milton** |
| ***Paradise Regained*** (1671) | Milton |
| ***Ramayana*** / ***Mahabharata*** | **Valmiki** / **Vyasa** |
| ***Shahnameh*** | **Ferdowsi** (Persian) |
| ***Meghnad Badh Kabya*** (1861) | **Michael Madhusudan Dutt** (Bangla; blank verse) |

**Mock epic / mock-heroic:** uses the grand epic style for a trivial subject. ***The Rape of the Lock*** by **Alexander Pope** (theft of a lock of **Belinda**'s hair by the Baron); Dryden's *Mac Flecknoe*; Pope's *The Dunciad*.

## Ballad 🔥
- A short **narrative song** passed down orally; simple language, dialogue, **refrain**, and the **ballad stanza** (quatrain, rhyme **abcb**, lines of 4 and 3 stresses).
- **Folk ballads:** "Sir Patrick Spens", "Chevy Chase", "Lord Randal", the Robin Hood ballads. Collected in Thomas **Percy**'s *Reliques of Ancient English Poetry* (1765).
- **Literary ballads:** Coleridge's "**The Rime of the Ancient Mariner**" (in ***Lyrical Ballads***, 1798, with Wordsworth; the albatross; "Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink"); Keats's "**La Belle Dame sans Merci**"; Wilde's "The Ballad of Reading Gaol".

## Other verse forms (quick table)
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Lyric** | Short poem expressing personal feeling |
| **Blank verse** | **Unrhymed iambic pentameter** (Milton, Shakespeare) |
| **Free verse** | No fixed metre or rhyme (Whitman) |
| **Couplet** / **heroic couplet** | Two rhyming lines / rhymed iambic pentameter pairs (Pope, Dryden) |
| **Quatrain / sestet / octave** | Stanza of 4 / 6 / 8 lines |
| **Terza rima** | aba bcb cdc… (Dante) |
| **Rhyme royal** | 7 lines, ababbcc (Chaucer) |
| **Spenserian stanza** | 9 lines, last one an alexandrine, ababbcbcc |
| **Villanelle** | 19 lines, two refrains |
| **Limerick** | 5 lines, aabba, humorous |
| **Haiku** | Japanese, 3 lines, 5-7-5 syllables |
| **Dramatic monologue** | One speaker to a silent listener (Browning's "**My Last Duchess**") |
| **Epitaph** | Lines written on a tomb |

## Quick revision
- Sonnet = **14 lines**; Petrarchan = **octave + sestet**; Shakespearean = **3 quatrains + couplet (abab cdcd efef gg)**.
- Sonnet introduced into English by **Wyatt**.
- *Lycidas* → **Edward King**; *Adonais* → **Keats**; *In Memoriam* → **Hallam**; *Thyrsis* → **Clough**.
- "Ode to the West Wind" = **Shelley**; "Ode to a Nightingale", "Grecian Urn" = **Keats**.
- Oldest English epic: ***Beowulf***; *Paradise Lost* = **Milton**; mock epic *The Rape of the Lock* = **Pope**.
- Ballad stanza rhyme: **abcb**; *Lyrical Ballads* (1798) = **Wordsworth & Coleridge**.

> **Why it matters:** Every BCS, bank and NTRCA paper asks 2–4 questions like "The idiom 'a white elephant' means…". The same idioms repeat year after year, so learn the table below thoroughly.

## How to learn
- An **idiom** is a group of words whose meaning cannot be guessed from the individual words.
- Learn by **picture + Bangla meaning**. Many idioms come from myths (Achilles' heel, Herculean task, Midas touch, Gordian knot) or animals (black sheep, dark horse, crocodile tears).

ENG-36.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask definitions ("A story with a second, symbolic meaning is…"), famous examples (*The Pilgrim's Progress*, *Gulliver's Travels*), and "Identify the figure of speech" in a quoted line.

## Allegory and related forms 🔥
- **Allegory:** a story in which characters and events stand for **abstract ideas or a second meaning** (moral, religious or political).

| Work | Author | Type of allegory |
|---|---|---|
| ***The Pilgrim's Progress*** (1678) 🔥 | **John Bunyan** | Religious; hero **Christian** travels from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City |
| ***The Faerie Queene*** | **Edmund Spenser** | Moral and political; each knight = a virtue |
| ***Everyman*** (15th c.) | Anonymous | **Morality play** |
| ***Animal Farm*** (1945) | **George Orwell** | Political (Russian Revolution) |
| ***Absalom and Achitophel*** (1681) | **John Dryden** | Political satire in biblical disguise |
| ***The Crucible*** | Arthur Miller | Salem trials = McCarthyism |

| Related term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Fable** | Short tale with animals, ending in a moral | **Aesop**'s fables |
| **Parable** | Short tale with a moral or spiritual lesson (human characters) | Parables of Jesus (the Prodigal Son) |
| **Symbol** | An object standing for an idea | Albatross in "The Ancient Mariner" |

## Satire 🔥
- **Satire:** literature that **ridicules** the follies and vices of people or society, to correct them. Tools: irony, sarcasm, parody, exaggeration.
- **Horatian satire:** gentle, amused (from Horace). **Juvenalian satire:** bitter, angry (from Juvenal).

| Work | Author | Target |
|---|---|---|
| ***Gulliver's Travels*** (1726) 🔥 | **Jonathan Swift** | Mankind and politics; **Lilliput** (tiny people), **Brobdingnag** (giants), **Laputa** (floating island of scientists), land of the **Houyhnhnms** (rational horses) and **Yahoos** (brutish humans) |
| "**A Modest Proposal**" (1729) | **Swift** | Irish poverty; ironically suggests eating babies |
| ***Mac Flecknoe***, ***Absalom and Achitophel*** | **Dryden** | Poet Shadwell / Whig politics |
| ***The Rape of the Lock***, ***The Dunciad*** | **Alexander Pope** | Fashionable society / dull writers |
| ***Hudibras*** | Samuel Butler | Puritans |
| ***Don Juan*** | **Lord Byron** | Society |
| ***Don Quixote*** | **Cervantes** | Chivalric romances |

| Related term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Parody** | Comic imitation of a particular work or style |
| **Burlesque** | Grotesque, comic treatment (high subject made low or low made high) |
| **Lampoon** | Harsh, personal satire on an individual |
| **Sarcasm** | Bitter, taunting remark |
| **Invective** | Direct abuse |

## Figures of speech 🔥🔥
| Figure | Definition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Simile** | Comparison using ***like / as*** | "**My love is like a red, red rose**" (Burns); "I wandered lonely **as** a cloud" (Wordsworth) |
| **Metaphor** | Implied comparison, no *like/as* | "**All the world's a stage**" (Shakespeare); "Life is a dream" |
| **Personification** | Giving human qualities to non-human things | "**Death lays his icy hand on kings**" (James Shirley) |
| **Apostrophe** | Addressing an absent person or a thing | "**Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour**" (Wordsworth); "O Death, where is thy sting?" |
| **Hyperbole** | Deliberate exaggeration | "**Ten thousand saw I at a glance**" (Wordsworth); "I have told you a million times" |
| **Metonymy** | A related thing stands for the thing meant | "**The pen is mightier than the sword**" (pen = writing, sword = force); "The **Crown**" = the king |
| **Synecdoche** | A part for the whole, or whole for part | "**All hands** on deck"; "our daily **bread**" (= food) |
| **Oxymoron** | Two opposite words **side by side** | "**bitter-sweet**", "**open secret**", "**O loving hate!**" (Romeo and Juliet), "cruel kindness" |
| **Paradox** | A statement that seems absurd but hides a truth | "**The Child is father of the Man**" (Wordsworth); "More haste, less speed" |
| **Antithesis** | Contrasting ideas in balanced phrases | "**Man proposes, God disposes**"; "**To err is human, to forgive divine**" (Pope) |
| **Alliteration** | Repetition of the **same initial consonant sound** | "**P**eter **P**iper **p**icked a **p**eck…"; "The **f**air breeze blew, the white foam **f**lew, / The **f**urrow **f**ollowed **f**ree" (Coleridge) |
| **Assonance** | Repetition of **vowel sounds** | "Hear the mellow wedding bells" |
| **Onomatopoeia** | Word imitating a sound | **buzz, hiss, murmur, crash, cuckoo** |
| **Climax** | Ideas in rising order of importance | "**I came, I saw, I conquered.**" |
| **Anticlimax / bathos** | Sudden fall from the important to the trivial | "Here thou, great Anna! whom three realms obey, / Dost sometimes counsel take—and sometimes tea." (Pope) |
| **Euphemism** | Mild word for an unpleasant idea | "He **passed away**" (= died) |
| **Litotes** | Understatement by denying the opposite | "He is **no fool**"; "not bad" |
| **Transferred epithet** | Adjective moved from the proper noun to another | "a **sleepless night**" (the person, not the night, is sleepless) |
| **Irony** | Meaning opposite to the words / result opposite to expectation | Verbal, situational, **dramatic irony** (audience knows more than the character) |
| **Pun** | Play on two meanings of a word | "Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a **grave** man" (Mercutio) |
| **Zeugma** | One word applied to two others in different senses | "She lost her hat and her temper" |
| **Rhetorical question** | Question asked for effect, no answer expected | "**If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?**" (Shelley) |

**Simile vs metaphor:** simile says *like/as*; metaphor says one thing *is* another.
**Oxymoron vs paradox:** oxymoron = two contradictory **words**; paradox = a contradictory **statement**.

## Other terms often asked
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Conceit** | Far-fetched, elaborate comparison; **metaphysical conceit** (Donne's compasses in "A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning") |
| **Catharsis** | Purging of **pity and fear** through tragedy (**Aristotle**, *Poetics*) |
| **Hamartia** | Tragic flaw / error of the hero |
| **Hubris** | Excessive pride |
| **Deus ex machina** | Sudden artificial solution to a plot |
| **Soliloquy** | Character speaks thoughts alone on stage ("To be, or not to be") |
| **Aside** | Short remark heard by the audience, not by other characters |
| **Poetic justice** | Virtue rewarded, vice punished (term by **Thomas Rymer**) |
| **Negative capability** | **Keats**'s term: accepting uncertainty without reaching after fact |
| **Objective correlative** | **T. S. Eliot**'s term |
| **Willing suspension of disbelief** | **Coleridge**'s phrase |
| **Bildungsroman** | Novel of growing up (e.g. *David Copperfield*) |
| **Picaresque novel** | Adventures of a roguish hero (*Tom Jones*, *Don Quixote*) |
| **Epistolary novel** | Novel in letters (Richardson's ***Pamela***, 1740) |

## Quick revision
- ***The Pilgrim's Progress*** = religious allegory by **Bunyan**; hero **Christian**.
- ***Gulliver's Travels*** (1726) = satire by **Swift**; Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Houyhnhnms, Yahoos.
- **Like/as** → simile; **no like/as** → metaphor.
- "The pen is mightier than the sword" → **metonymy**.
- "Bitter-sweet", "open secret" → **oxymoron**.
- "The Child is father of the Man" → **paradox**.
- "Death lays his icy hand on kings" → **personification**.
- "I came, I saw, I conquered" → **climax**.

ENG-37.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Bank and BCS papers regularly ask "*Put off* means…" or "Fill in: The meeting was called ___." A **group verb (phrasal verb)** is a verb + preposition/adverb whose meaning changes, e.g. *give up* = abandon.

## Key tips
- The particle changes the meaning: **look after** (take care of) vs **look for** (search) vs **look into** (investigate).
- Most-tested verbs: **look, put, give, take, break, bring, call, come, get, make, run, set, turn**.

> **Why it matters:** 2–4 synonym questions appear in almost every BCS, bank, NTRCA and primary-teacher paper ("The synonym of *candid* is…"). The words below are the ones that repeat most often.

## Tips
- Know the **exact** meaning, not just a vague idea: *eminent* (famous) vs *imminent* (about to happen).
- Eliminate antonyms first; examiners often put the antonym among the options.
- Learn words in **families**: *abundant, copious, ample, plentiful*.

## Antonyms with negative prefixes
| Prefix | Rule / examples |
|---|---|
| **un-** | happy → **unhappy**; able → **unable**; fair → **unfair** |
| **in-** | active → **inactive**; correct → **incorrect**; visible → **invisible** |
| **im-** (before b, m, p) | possible → **impossible**; mortal → **immortal**; balance → **imbalance** |
| **il-** (before l) | legal → **illegal**; literate → **illiterate**; logical → **illogical** |
| **ir-** (before r) | regular → **irregular**; responsible → **irresponsible**; relevant → **irrelevant** |
| **dis-** | honest → **dishonest**; agree → **disagree**; loyal → **disloyal** |
| **mis-** | understand → **misunderstand**; fortune → **misfortune** |
| **non-** | violence → **non-violence**; sense → **nonsense** |
| **mal-** | nutrition → **malnutrition**; function → **malfunction** |

Traps: the opposite of *flammable* is **non-flammable** (**inflammable** means the same as *flammable*). *Immoral* = against morals; *amoral* = without moral sense.

ENG-42.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask "firsts" (first Asian, first woman, first African), laureates who declined the prize, famous works of laureates, and the latest winner. The latest-winner question changes every year, so keep it updated.

## Basic facts 🔥
- Founded by the will of **Alfred Nobel** (Swedish chemist, inventor of **dynamite**; died **1896**).
- First awarded in **1901**. Prize ceremony on **10 December** (Nobel's death anniversary).
- The literature prize is awarded by the **Swedish Academy** (Stockholm). The laureate is usually announced in **early October**.
- Not awarded in some years, e.g. **1914, 1918, 1935, 1940–1943**. The **2018** prize was announced in **2019** (together with the 2019 prize) after a scandal at the Academy.

ENG-43.notes:
> **Why it matters:** "Which word is correctly spelt?" appears in most BCS, bank and primary-teacher papers. The same tricky words (accommodation, committee, millennium, questionnaire…) are asked again and again.

## Useful spelling rules 🔥
| Rule | Examples |
|---|---|
| **i before e, except after c** (when the sound is "ee") | believe, achieve, niece / **receive, deceive, ceiling, receipt, conceive** |
| Exceptions to the i–e rule | **seize, weird, either, neither, leisure, foreign, height** |
| **Drop silent -e** before a vowel suffix | hope → hoping, write → writing, argue → **argument**, true → **truly** |
| **Keep -e** after *c/g* before *-able/-ous* (soft sound) | **noticeable, changeable, manageable, courageous** |
| **Double the final consonant** (short vowel + stressed last syllable) | begin → **beginning**, occur → **occurred, occurrence**, refer → **referred**, commit → **committed** |
| No doubling if the stress moves or is not on the last syllable | benefit → **benefited**, offer → **offered**, travel → travelled (UK) / traveled (US) |
| **Consonant + y → i** | happy → happiness, carry → carried; but play → played |
| **-ful** has one *l* | beautiful, careful, **successful**; but **fulfil** (UK) / fulfill (US) |
| **-cede / -ceed / -sede** | only **supersede** ends in -sede; **exceed, proceed, succeed** end in -ceed; others end in -cede (precede, concede) |

> **Why it matters:** Bank (especially Bangladesh Bank AD/Officer) and some BCS papers ask "DOCTOR : HOSPITAL :: TEACHER : ?". The trick is to name the **exact relationship** in the first pair and find the option with the **same** relationship in the same order.

## How to solve (3 steps)
1. Make a sentence with the first pair: "A **doctor works in** a **hospital**."
2. Put each option into the same sentence: "A **teacher works in** a **school**." ✔
3. If two options fit, make the sentence more specific. Keep the **same order** (A is to B as C is to D).

| **Worker : workplace** | Doctor : Hospital | Teacher : School |

ENG-48.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask you to identify the kind of clause ("The underlined part is a noun/adjective/adverb clause"), choose the right relative pronoun (who/whom/whose/which/that), and combine sentences.

## Basics
- A **clause** is a group of words with a **subject and a finite verb**. A **phrase** has no finite verb.
  - *in the morning* → phrase. *when the sun rose* → clause.
- **Principal (main / independent) clause:** can stand alone.
- **Subordinate (dependent) clause:** cannot stand alone; works as a **noun, adjective or adverb**.
- Sentence types: **simple** (one main clause), **compound** (two main clauses + *and, but, or, so*), **complex** (main clause + subordinate clause).

## 1. Noun clause 🔥
Does the work of a **noun**. Usually begins with **that, what, whether, if, who, why, how, where, when, whatever**.

| Function | Example |
|---|---|
| **Subject** of a verb | **What he said** is true. / **That he is honest** is known to all. |
| **Object** of a verb | I know **that he is honest**. / Tell me **where you live**. |
| **Object of a preposition** | Pay attention to **what the teacher says**. |
| **Complement** of a verb | This is **what I wanted**. / The truth is **that he failed**. |
| **In apposition** to a noun | The news **that he had died** shocked us. |

Test: replace the clause with "it" or "this". *I know it.* → noun clause.

## 2. Adjective (relative) clause 🔥
Qualifies a **noun or pronoun**, usually coming right after it. Begins with a **relative pronoun** (**who, whom, whose, which, that**) or **relative adverb** (**where, when, why**).

| Relative word | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **who** | person, subject | The man **who came here** is my uncle. |
| **whom** | person, object | The boy **whom you punished** is innocent. |
| **whose** | possession | This is the girl **whose father is a doctor**. |
| **which** | things, animals | The pen **which I bought** is lost. |
| **that** | persons or things (defining clauses) | This is the house **that Jack built**. |
| **where** | place | This is the village **where I was born**. |
| **when** | time | I remember the day **when we met**. |
| **why** | reason | Tell me the reason **why you are late**. |

Rules:
- **Defining (restrictive)** clause: no commas; needed to identify the noun. *Students who work hard succeed.*
- **Non-defining (non-restrictive)** clause: with commas; extra information. *My father, **who is a doctor**, lives in Khulna.* Do **not** use *that* here.
- **That** is preferred after **superlatives, all, only, none, nothing, everything**: *He is the best man **that** I know. All **that** glitters is not gold.*

Noun clause vs adjective clause (same word *that*):
- *The news **that he won** is true.* → **noun clause** (apposition; "that" is only a conjunction).
- *The news **that he brought** is true.* → **adjective clause** ("that" = which, object of *brought*).

## 3. Adverb clause 🔥
Modifies a **verb, adjective or adverb**; tells when, where, why, how, on what condition, etc.

| Kind | Conjunctions | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | when, while, before, after, since, until, as soon as | Wait **until I return**. |
| **Place** | where, wherever | Go **wherever you like**. |
| **Reason / cause** | because, since, as | He was absent **because he was ill**. |
| **Purpose** | so that, in order that, lest | He works hard **so that he may succeed**. |
| **Result** | so … that, such … that | He is **so** weak **that he cannot walk**. |
| **Condition** | if, unless, provided | **If you run**, you will catch the bus. |
| **Concession / contrast** | though, although, even if | **Though he is poor**, he is honest. |
| **Comparison** | than, as … as | He is taller **than I am**. |
| **Manner** | as, as if, as though | Do **as I tell you**. |

Test: the clause answers **when / where / why / how / under what condition**.

## Identifying quickly
| Sentence | Clause type |
|---|---|
| I know **where he lives**. | Noun (object of *know*) |
| This is the house **where he lives**. | Adjective (qualifies *house*) |
| Stay **where you are**. | Adverb (place, modifies *stay*) |

Same word *where*, three different clauses: the job the clause does decides its type.

## Quick revision
- Clause = subject + finite verb; phrase has no finite verb.
- **Noun clause** = subject / object / complement / apposition; test with "it".
- **Adjective clause** follows a noun: **who, whom, whose, which, that, where, when, why**.
- **Adverb clause** tells time, place, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession, comparison, manner.
- Non-defining clauses take **commas** and never *that*.
- Use **that** after superlatives, *all, only, nothing*.

ENG-49.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Gap-filling questions test the right modal (*must, should, ought to, may, might, need, dare, used to*) and causative patterns (*have it done, get him to do, make him do*). These are common in bank and BCS papers.

## Modal auxiliaries: rules
- Modals: **can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to**; semi-modals: **need, dare, used to**.
- A modal is followed by the **bare infinitive (V1)**: *He can **swim**.* (✗ can swims, ✗ can to swim) — except **ought to** and **used to**.
- Modals have **no -s** in the third person: *She **must** go.*
- Modals do not take *do* in questions/negatives: *Can he swim? He cannot swim.*

## Uses of each modal 🔥
| Modal | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **can** | ability (present), permission (informal) | I **can** speak English. **Can** I go now? |
| **could** | past ability; polite request | He **could** run fast as a boy. **Could** you help me? |
| **may** | permission (formal); possibility | **May** I come in, sir? It **may** rain today. |
| **might** | weaker possibility; past of *may* | He **might** come, but I doubt it. |
| **may** (wish) | prayer / wish | **May** you live long! **May** Allah bless you. |
| **shall** | future with I/we (formal); offers; command in law | **Shall** I open the window? |
| **should** | duty, advice | You **should** respect your parents. |
| **ought to** | moral duty, obligation | We **ought to** help the poor. |
| **will** | future; willingness | I **will** help you. |
| **would** | past habit; polite request; conditional | He **would** walk by the river every evening. **Would** you mind waiting? |
| **must** | strong necessity; logical certainty | You **must** obey the law. He **must** be tired after the journey. |
| **must not** | prohibition | You **must not** smoke here. |
| **need not** | absence of necessity | You **need not** come tomorrow. |
| **dare** | courage | How **dare** you insult me? He **dare not** go there. |
| **used to** | past habit (no longer true) | I **used to** play football. |

**Must not vs need not:** *must not* = it is forbidden; *need not* = it is not necessary.
**Need / dare** as modals are used mainly in **negatives and questions**: *Need he go? He need not go.* As main verbs they take *to*: *He needs to go.*

## Perfect modals (modal + have + V3) 🔥
| Form | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **should have + V3** | duty not done in the past (regret) | You **should have come** earlier. |
| **must have + V3** | strong logical conclusion about the past | The road is wet; it **must have rained**. |
| **could have + V3** | past ability/possibility not used | You **could have won** the match. |
| **may / might have + V3** | past possibility | He **may have missed** the bus. |
| **need not have + V3** | did something unnecessary | You **need not have bought** milk; we had plenty. |
| **would have + V3** | third conditional | I **would have helped** you if I had known. |

## Causative verbs 🔥
Used when someone **causes** another person to do something.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **have + person + V1** | arrange for someone to do | I **had the mechanic repair** my car. |
| **have + thing + V3** | get something done by someone | I **had my car repaired**. I **had my hair cut**. |
| **get + person + to + V1** | persuade someone to do | I **got him to sign** the paper. |
| **get + thing + V3** | same as *have + thing + V3* | She **got her watch mended**. |
| **make + person + V1** (no *to*) | force | The teacher **made him stand** up. |
| **let + person + V1** (no *to*) | allow | **Let** him **go**. Father **let** me **use** his car. |
| **help + person + (to) V1** | assist (both correct) | He **helped me (to) carry** the bag. |

Passive of **make**: *to* comes back.
- Active: *They **made** him **work**.* → Passive: *He **was made to work**.*

Common exam items:
- ✓ *I had my **photograph taken**.* ✗ *I had my photograph take.*
- ✓ *He made me **laugh**.* ✗ *He made me to laugh.*
- ✓ *I got him **to repair** it.* ✗ *I got him repair it.*

## Quick revision
- Modal + **bare V1**; only **ought to / used to** take *to*.
- **May** = permission, possibility, wish ("May you live long").
- **Must not** = prohibited; **need not** = not necessary.
- **Should have + V3** = regret about the past; **must have + V3** = certain deduction.
- **have / get + thing + V3**: I had my hair **cut**.
- **make / let + person + V1** (no *to*); **get + person + to V1**.
- Passive: He **was made to** work.

ENG-50.notes:
> **Why it matters:** BCS written and preliminary papers, NTRCA and bank exams give an unpunctuated passage or ask "Which sentence is correctly punctuated/capitalized?". A few rules on commas, apostrophes, quotation marks and capital letters cover most questions.

## Punctuation marks at a glance
| Mark | Name | Main use |
|---|---|---|
| . | **Full stop (period)** | End of a statement or command; abbreviations (Mr., Dr., e.g.) |
| , | **Comma** | Short pause; lists; after introductory words; around extra information |
| ; | **Semicolon** | Joins two closely related independent clauses; separates items that already contain commas |
| : | **Colon** | Introduces a list, explanation or quotation |
| ? | **Question (interrogation) mark** | End of a direct question |
| ! | **Exclamation (note of exclamation)** | Strong feeling; after interjections |
| ' | **Apostrophe** | Possession; contractions |
| " " / ' ' | **Quotation marks (inverted commas)** | Direct speech; quoted words; titles of short works |
| - | **Hyphen** | Joins parts of a compound word (well-known, mother-in-law) |
| — | **Dash** | Sudden break or added comment |
| ( ) | **Brackets (parentheses)** | Extra information |

## Comma rules 🔥
1. **Lists:** *I bought rice, fish, eggs and vegetables.* (The comma before *and*, called the Oxford/serial comma, is optional.)
2. **Addressing someone (vocative):** *Rahim, come here.* / *Come here, Rahim.*
3. **After introductory words/clauses:** *However, he did not come.* / *If it rains, we will stay home.*
4. **Non-defining clause / apposition:** *Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, is crowded.* / *My father, who is a doctor, lives in Khulna.*
5. **Before a coordinating conjunction joining two long clauses:** *He worked hard, but he failed.*
6. **Before and after direct speech tags:** *He said, "I am busy."* / *"I am busy," he said.*
7. **Yes/No, interjections:** *Yes, I will go.* / *Alas, he is dead!* (or *Alas! he is dead.*)
8. **Dates and addresses:** *1 October 2026*; *Mirpur, Dhaka*.

## Semicolon and colon
- **Semicolon:** *He was ill; he could not attend the meeting.* / *Man proposes; God disposes.*
- Before words like *however, therefore* joining two clauses: *He was tired; however, he kept working.*
- **Colon:** *You need three things: patience, practice and hard work.* / *Remember this: honesty is the best policy.*

## Apostrophe 🔥
| Use | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Singular possessive | **'s** | the boy**'s** book |
| Plural ending in -s | only **'** | the boys**'** hostel |
| Plural not ending in -s | **'s** | the children**'s** park, women**'s** rights |
| Joint possession | 's on the last noun | Rahim and Karim**'s** shop (one shop) |
| Separate possession | 's on each noun | Rahim**'s** and Karim**'s** shops |
| Contraction | letters left out | don't, it's (= it is), can't |
| **its vs it's** 🔥 | *its* = possessive (no apostrophe); *it's* = it is | The dog wagged **its** tail. **It's** raining. |

Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: **yours, hers, ours, theirs, its**.

## Quotation marks and direct speech
- *He said, "**I** am going home."* → comma before the quote, capital letter to start the quoted sentence, full stop **inside** the quotation marks.
- *"Where are you going?" she asked.* → question mark inside, because the quotation itself is a question.

## Capitalization rules 🔥
Use a **capital letter** for:
1. The **first word of a sentence** and of a direct quotation.
2. The pronoun **I** (always).
3. **Proper nouns:** names of people, places, rivers, mountains, organisations: *Rahim, Dhaka, the Padma, the Himalayas, the United Nations*.
4. **Days, months, festivals:** *Friday, October, Eid, Pohela Boishakh*. (Seasons are usually lower case: *spring, winter*.)
5. **Nationalities, languages, religions:** *Bangladeshi, English, Islam, Muslim, Hindu*.
6. **Titles before names:** *Dr. Yunus, President Lincoln* (but *the president of the club*).
7. **Main words in titles** of books, films, etc.: *The Old Man and the Sea*.
8. **God** and names of holy books: *God, the Quran, the Bible*.
9. **Historical events, periods, documents:** *the Liberation War, the Renaissance, the Constitution*.
10. **Abbreviations/acronyms:** *UN, BCS, NATO, UNESCO*.
11. **Geographical directions as regions** (not as directions): *the Middle East, North Bengal* but *go north*.

## Worked example
Unpunctuated: *rahim said to karim where are you going*
Correct: **Rahim said to Karim, "Where are you going?"**

Unpunctuated: *alas my friend is dead said he*
Correct: **"Alas! My friend is dead," said he.**

## Quick revision
- Full stop inside the quotation marks; comma before the opening quote.
- **it's** = it is; **its** = possessive.
- boy's (one), boys' (many), children's (plural without -s).
- Semicolon joins two complete, related clauses.
- Colon introduces a list or explanation.
- Always capitalize **I**, proper nouns, days, months, languages, God.
- Seasons usually take small letters.

ENG-52.notes:
> **Why it matters:** Exams ask "The noun form of *decide* is…", "The adjective of *courage* is…", "The verb of *strong* is…", and "Which prefix makes the opposite of *regular*?". Knowing the common prefixes and suffixes answers these quickly.

## A. Prefixes (added at the beginning)
### Negative prefixes 🔥
| Prefix | Rule / meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **un-** | not | unhappy, unable, unfair |
| **in-** | not | inactive, incomplete, invisible |
| **im-** | before **b, m, p** | impossible, immortal, imbalance, impatient |
| **il-** | before **l** | illegal, illiterate, illogical |
| **ir-** | before **r** | irregular, irrelevant, irresponsible |
| **dis-** | not / opposite | dishonest, disagree, disappear |
| **non-** | not | non-violence, nonsense, non-resident |
| **mis-** | wrongly | misunderstand, mislead, misuse |
| **mal-** | badly | malnutrition, malpractice, malfunction |
| **a- / an-** | without | amoral, atheist, anarchy |
| **anti-** | against | antisocial, antibiotic, anticlimax |
| **counter-** | against, opposite | counterattack, counterpart |

### Number prefixes 🔥
| Prefix | Number | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **uni- / mono-** | one | uniform, unicorn, monologue, monopoly, monogamy |
| **bi- / di-** | two | bicycle, bilingual, biennial, dioxide |
| **tri-** | three | triangle, tricolour, trilogy |
| **quad- / tetra-** | four | quadrangle, tetrahedron |
| **penta-** | five | pentagon |
| **hexa-** | six | hexagon |
| **dec- / deca-** | ten | decade, decathlon |
| **cent-** | hundred | century, centenary |
| **milli-** | thousand(th) | millennium, millimetre |
| **semi- / hemi- / demi-** | half | semicircle, hemisphere, demigod |
| **multi- / poly-** | many | multinational, polygon, polygamy |

### Other common prefixes
| Prefix | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **pre-** | before | prewar, preview, prehistoric |
| **post-** | after | postwar, postpone, postgraduate |
| **ante-** | before | antedate, antenatal |
| **re-** | again, back | rewrite, return, rebuild |
| **sub-** | under | submarine, subway, subtitle |
| **super-** | above | superman, supernatural |
| **inter-** | between | international, interview |
| **intra-** | within | intranet, intravenous |
| **trans-** | across | transport, transatlantic |
| **over- / under-** | too much / too little | overwork / underpaid |
| **co- / com- / con-** | together | co-operate, compose, connect |
| **ex-** | former; out | ex-president; export |
| **auto-** | self | autobiography, automatic |
| **tele-** | far | telephone, television |
| **micro- / macro-** | small / large | microscope / macroeconomics |
| **en- / em-** | make, put into (forms verbs) | enlarge, enrich, endanger, empower |
| **be-** | make (forms verbs) | befriend, belittle |

## B. Suffixes (added at the end)
| Forms | Suffixes | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Nouns** | -ness, -ment, -tion/-sion, -ity, -hood, -ship, -dom, -ism, -ance/-ence, -er/-or, -ist, -ee | kindness, development, decision, ability, childhood, friendship, freedom, heroism, importance, teacher, scientist, employee |
| **Adjectives** | -ful, -less, -able/-ible, -ous, -ive, -al, -ic, -ish, -y, -ly (adjective) | useful, careless, readable, dangerous, active, national, historic, childish, cloudy, friendly |
| **Verbs** | -ize/-ise, -en, -fy, -ate | modernize, strengthen, beautify, activate |
| **Adverbs** | -ly, -wise, -ward(s) | quickly, clockwise, backward |

Watch out: **childish** (silly, negative) vs **childlike** (innocent, positive); **historic** (important in history) vs **historical** (related to history); **economic** vs **economical** (thrifty).

## Quick revision
- **il-** before l, **ir-** before r, **im-** before b/m/p.
- **en-** makes verbs: enlarge, enrich, endanger, encourage.
- **-en** makes verbs: strengthen, widen, deepen, lengthen.
- **strong → strength, wide → width, deep → depth, high → height**.
- **pronounce → pronunciation**; **maintain → maintenance**.
- **die → death → dead**; **lose → loss**; **choose → choice**.
- **poor → poverty**; **humble → humility**; **wise → wisdom**.

> **Why it matters:** BCS preliminary and written papers, and especially bank exams, use words from English dailies (The Daily Star, The Business Standard, New Age) in synonym, gap-fill and comprehension questions. These words cover economy, politics, law, crime, disaster and diplomacy.

## A. Economy & finance 🔥

## Quick revision
- **Remittance** = money sent by expatriate workers.
- **Inflation** = rising prices; **stagflation** = inflation + stagnation.
- **Incumbent** = present office-holder.
- **Nepotism** = favouring relatives.
- **Repatriation** = sending refugees home.
- **Arson** = deliberate setting of fire; **extortion** = চাঁদাবাজি.
- **Sanction / embargo** = penalties on trade/country.
- **Verdict** = court decision; **acquittal** = released as not guilty.
